speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Defence Production):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: C. D. HOWE COMPANY LIMITED REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF THE LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege. On Tuesday last, during my absence from Ottawa, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) made certain statements on the radio, and on Wednesday a debate occurred in this house in which my name was mentioned. This same matter had been raised in the house some time ago. I made a very short statement then, but I think the house is entitled to a more complete statement at this time. I might add that I make this statement on my responsibility as a member of parliament and as a member of this government.
The paragraph to which I refer in the broadcast-this purports to be the script of that broadcast-reads:
We found out last week after considerable effort that Mr. Howe has arranged government contracts with his own family company, C. D. Howe Company Limited, which will give that company more than five hundred thousand dollars in fees. Those contracts were secretly arranged without tender and without competition.
I have stated in the house that I have had no connection with C. D. Howe Company Limited since 1935. The circumstances then were that I was asked to contest a seat in parliament; Mr. Mackenzie King pressed me to accept the nomination, and I told him I would do so if I could divest myself of my interest in C. D. Howe Company Limited. At that time I owned all the shares of the company. I called in the man 1 thought was capable of carrying on the work of the company, and talked over the matter with him. I may say it is not easy for a man to divest himself of an association that has continued for twenty years. I had gathered together a very competent staff, many of whom I had brought to Port Arthur, and many of whom had homes there. I also had a responsibility to a number of my clients, some in Canada and a few outside Canada, in that we were custodians of the plans of the various structures we had designed for them and it was our duty to keep those plans and calculations available for their use.
In any case I decided that I could not divest myself of the company unless I could arrange for the company to continue. I talked the matter over with this man, one of my senior engineers, and he thought he could carry on if he could use the company name. He said he would not undertake to carry on if he had to start afresh and operate the company under another name. I was rather reluctant to make that arrangement; however, I thought any personal objections I might have should be overlooked in the overriding interest of keeping the company in operation, and it was agreed that the name could be used. It was decided to form a group of competent men to take over the shares of the company. I sold all the shares in the company to that group. I sold them at a nominal price which represented the cash which was invested in the company at that moment. No one in that group had any connection with the Howe family; they were neither members of the family nor related in any way, directly or indirectly, to any member of the Howe family.
That arrangement was completed before nomination day in 1935. I allowed myself to be nominated knowing I was free from any connection with C. D. Howe Company Limited. None of us has enough foresight, but if I had known what was to happen subsequently I think I would not have allowed my name to be used. I am sure the company would not have wanted to use that name, because of the embarrassment it has caused the company subsequently.
I have given no business whatever to C. D. Howe Company, outside of the business that must flow to it anyway. They are the only firm in Canada that specializes in grain elevator work. They have been doing the work of the board of grain commissioners since the inception of the board. I noticed that in the years 1930 to 1935 the company collected $89,000 in fees for work performed for the board of grain commissioners. The company has continued to do work for the board of grain commissioners, even when that board has been my responsibility, as it has been for the last two or three years. I looked over the list of recent jobs, and they each represented work carrying a fee of less than $6,000, although in the aggregate the fees over the last sixteen years, while less than those collected in the five years of the Bennett regime, were still a substantial sum.

C. D. Howe Company Limited
However, during world war II, every engineering company of any standing had government contracts, with the one exception of C. D. Howe Company. The firm did not ask me for participation in government war contracts, nor did I call on the firm for work of that kind. That was one of the penalties that we both paid, and I suggest the government paid, in a way, from the fact the firm carries my name.
Now, I come to the family side. I might say I do not like to discuss my family in this House of Commons. I have always tried to separate my family affairs from public life. Members may have noticed that my wife does not appear on the political platform, and that my family are not active politically. However, in 1945 Captain Stedman returned from overseas. He came back, with a fine war record and a Military Cross, to resume his studies in the university of Toronto. He completed an engineering course which was interrupted by the war. While he was in the university of Toronto, he married my daughter. When he took his degree in mechanical engineering in 1947 he applied to the C. D. Howe Company Limited fox work. I might say it has been the practice of the company, ever since I started it, to take a few graduates each year from Canadian universities. In fact, practically all the engineers in the company came from that source. Stedman applied for work with the company. I do not know why. Perhaps my daughter liked the idea of going back to Port Arthur where she was born and brought up. His application was accepted, and he joined the firm at the usual beginner's salary. That was in 1947, four years ago.
In 1948 my youngest son graduated from McGill as a civil engineer. He also applied to the C. D. Howe Company for a job, perhaps for the same reason. His application was accepted and he went to work with the C. D. Howe Company Limited at the usual starting salary. These men are still with the firm. I suppose the firm has at least fifty engineers, and some of them have seniority of at least twenty-five or thirty years. These boys have seniority in the firm consistent with their length of service with the firm. If that makes the C. D. Howe Company Limited a family company, my idea of a family company and that of the leader of the opposition are vastly different. That is the association of the family with the C. D. Howe Company Limited.
Certain statements were made in the debate that perhaps should receive comment. The leader of the opposition said he used the term "family company" advisedly, "because my son and son-in-law are actively engaged in

the company", and he said he understood that a son and son-in-law are members of the family. Then he mentioned the fact that when the matter was brought up in the house originally he talked of nepotism. Well, I got that reference, but it took a little time to penetrate. By that time the debate had moved on to something else. At the time I thought he was referring to another son of mine, William Howe. I might say that the name "William Howe" has been used in every French constituency in which a Conservative member has been the speaker, and has been freely used in the French language press. I might as well tell you about my son William Howe.
In 1940 my son William Howe, at the age of seventeen, enlisted as a midshipman in the Canadian navy. He has served continuously in the navy since that day, and is still serving in the Canadian navy. He has never at any time had any association or interest in the firm of C. D. Howe Company Limited.
Just to make the story complete, I have two other daughters whom I have not mentioned. One of them is married and lives in Montreal, and the other is a war widow living in Halifax. Neither of them has ever had any association with or interest in the firm of C. D. Howe Company Limited.
Now, we come to the two contracts that have been mentioned here. One was the contract for the Department of Public Works to design and supervise the construction of a dock at Seven Islands. I can say quite honestly that I never knew the company had that contract until after the agreement had been signed. I asked the deputy minister of public works why he gave the contract to the company, and he said the reason was that the company had a contract from a private firm to build a dock at Seven Islands, and so were working in that locality. For that reason he thought they were the logical firm to undertake the work. Then we have the contract with the national research council for the atomic pile at Chalk River. I knew about that contract. Dr. Mackenzie, president of the council, came to me and said he would like to give the work at Chalk River to the C. D. Howe Company Limited. I asked him why. He said that he had tried to place it with Defence Industries Limited, the firm that designed the original pile, but they had so much work in hand on projects of their own that they were unable to take the work. I said, "Who else is in the field?" He said, "We know of no Canadian engineering firm that has the experience in the structural, mechanical and electrical branches of engineering that are required on this job other than C. D.

Howe Company Limited." I said, "Why do you ask me about it? The national research council is an autonomous body; its charter provides that it shall place its own contracts, and no reference to the government is necessary. It has not been your practice to refer contracts to the government." He said, "Just for one reason, and that is that the firm bears your name. I shall not do it if it is going to be embarrassing to you." I said, "It is embarrassing, but is that the most important consideration? What will you do if you cannot get C. D. Howe Company Limited?" He said, "We shall have to go to the United States and get our engineering there." I thought the matter over and I said, "You need not worry about embarrassing C. D. Howe. I will take care of that. If the right thing to do is to give this job to the C. D. Howe Company Limited, give it to them." That is the last I heard of the matter, and the job was duly awarded.
Either the radio statement or the statement in the house mentioned that for these two jobs the company will receive fees of $500,000. I looked that up and found that the fee for the Chalk River pile is 1-07 per cent of $20 million, which is the agreed cost stated in the contract. This would give the company a little over $200,000. I do not know how big the dock job at Seven Islands is, but I suppose the fee on that would be five per cent gross, from which expenses have to be paid by the firm. That might be five per cent of $600,000, and if that is the amount, the fee would be $30,000. I would therefore judge that the statement that fees were $500,000 for those two jobs is at least double the amount represented by the actual situation.
That is the story. I think I have given all the facts. If the leader of the opposition wishes to carry the matter further, I think he should adopt the practice that has been standard in this parliament and in every British parliament for many years past, namely, that he should rise in his place, make a charge, and stake his seat on his ability to prove the charge. If he is willing to do that, it is immaterial to me whether the charge is investigated by the public accounts committee, by a special committee of this house, or by a royal commission. I would point out to him that I am staking my seat in parliament on the accuracy of the statement I have just made to this House of Commons.
This is not the first time that smear tactics have been used by the leader of the opposition against myself. Hon. members will recall the broadcast made in the last federal election campaign in which he accused me of
C. D. Howe Company Limited taking graft from Canadair, and also of having other improper relations with that company. His charge was denied by every director of Canadair individually and publicly; and incidentally some of the directors were his own supporters. Later the Canadair transaction was investigated by the public accounts committee of this house. The leader of the opposition himself was a member of that public accounts committee at the time. The public accounts committee brought in a unanimous report to this house. That report contained no criticism of the transaction so far as the government's interest was concerned. I suggest to hon. members that this is a further smear tactic against myself. While I do not worry too much about it, I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that I was entitled to make this statement of the position.

The amounts to be paid on the basis of percentages stated in relation to the stated amounts of the contracts: Sept lies, still to be paid, $41,813.60; Chalk River reactor, $294,274.58; board of grain commissioners, $208.00; national harbours board, $17,000, making a total of $353,296.18, or a grand total of $513,905.03; and it was to that figure that I referred.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has quite clearly indicated the association of his family with the company, and since he has brought that up, then he has established exactly what was said.

maintopic: C. D. HOWE COMPANY LIMITED REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF THE LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
speechtext:
In so far as the Seven Islands job is concerned, when the Seven Islands job was undertaken the C. D. Howe Company Limited opened offices at 1421 Atwater street in Montreal, which was formerly the office of War Assets Corporation. Then I find that in the Advertising Journal of January, 1951, there is this advertisement:
Wanted-20 graduate engineers and draftsmen, mechanical, civil and electrical for projects in Ontario and Quebec by C. D. Howe Limited, 1421 Atwater street, Montreal, Quebec.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce is well aware that the member of his family in whom he has such confidence-and this is not in question-is pretty actively associated with a responsible position with that office that has been opened up in Montreal. These are the contracts that form the substantial basis of the work that is now being done by this company.
When the question is raised about "smear" tactics-and my remarks in this respect apply with equal force to the Prime Minister- before talking about smear tactics it is time that the government cleaned up this improper situation, and made it clear that no further contracts of this kind will be awarded. And that does not apply only to members of families, but also to friends, political and otherwise; because there has been a long established principle in regard to matters of this kind which is of the utmost importance at any time, but which assumes added importance when under any emergency or so-called emergency situation, the government, or any minister of the government, is placed in the position where he can exercise wide powers, not under the continuing supervision of parliament, as a result of the emergency powers conferred upon him. That is the situation in which the Minister of Defence Production is placed today.
The members of this house, by a majority vote, imposed upon the Minister of Defence Production the responsibility for the supervision of contracts running into hundreds of millions of dollars, which, by the very nature of those contracts, are not brought before this house for discussion. At the present time, as was pointed out, there are contracts, for instance, being awarded across Canada for the construction of radar stations involving very large expenditures. In the very nature of things those stations are not discussed in detail here in this house. I am not suggesting they should be; but the very fact that operations of that kind, and other operations of a similar nature-and many of those operations are carried out at the request of the Department of National Defence by the Department of Defence Production-cannot be discussed, having regard to the nature
C. D. Howe Company Limited of their activities, does impose a special obligation upon the Minister of Defence Production to leave no doubt that there shall be no contracts awarded which in any way would offend the strict and unwritten rule that there shall be no advantage to any member of a family or friend of any member of the government in connection with contracts awarded in that way.
That principle has been so deeply embedded in the practices of our British parliamentary system that the time has long since passed when it was necessary to restate them, but it obviously is. They were as clearly stated as I have found them anywhere by Mr. Asquith at the time of the famous Marconi scandal in Britain, and I should like to quote from what he said about that situation. I am reading now from Mr. Asquith's own report of what took place at that time, and his enunciation of the principles which had been broadly accepted in regard to matters of this kind. He said this:
I took the opportunity to formulate rules, which I divided into two categories of rules of obligations and rules of prudence.
The first, of course, and the most obvious, is that (1) ministers ought not to enter into any transaction whereby their private pecuniary interests might, even conceivably, come into conflict with their public duty. There is no dispute about that. Again (2) no minister is justified, under any circumstances, in using official information, information that has come to him as a minister, for his own private profit or for that of his friends. Further (3), no minister ought to allow or put himself in a position to be tempted to use his official influence in support of any scheme, or in furtherance of any contract, in regard to which he has an undisclosed private interest. That again is beyond dispute. Again (4), no minister ought to accept from persons who are in negotiation with or seeking to enter into contractual or proprietary or pecuniary relations with the state, any kind of favour. That, I think, is also beyond dispute.
I will add a further proposition, which I am not sure has been completely formulated, though it has no doubt been adumbrated in the course of these debates, and that is that (5) ministers should scrupulously avoid speculative investments in securities as to which, from their position and their special means of early or confidential information, they have, or may have, an advantage over other people in anticipating market changes.
These, Mr. Speaker, were what Mr. Asquith described as rules of obligation and rules of prudence.

Mr. Speaker, I am continuing
to quote from what Mr. Asquith said at that time:
I think that in addition to those rules, which I have described as rules of obligation-because it seems to me that they have an ethical value and sanction, as well as being based on grounds of expediency and policy-there are, or there certainly ought to be, rules of prudence specially applicable to ministers and to persons in positions of official
[Mr. Maltais.l
responsibility, rules which perhaps never have been formulated, and which it would be very difficult to formulate in precise or universal terms. One of those rules is that in these matters such persons should carefully avoid all transactions which can give colour or countenance to the belief that they are doing anything which the rules of obligation forbid.
I have read this quotation because, so far as I can ascertain, that was the last time it became necessary, either in the House of Commons at Westminster or in the House of Commons here, to state in such clear and explicit terms the rules of prudence and the rules of obligation which have come down by trial and error, with centuries of precedent, under our type of parliamentary system.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has indicated that if he had thought there might be the association between himself and the government and the public that has happened, then he might have questioned the wisdom of continuing the use of that name. That is exactly the point before us.
When a minister has the immense power that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has, powers conferred upon him because it was stated that these wider powers would be necessary so that the government could deal with price controls and other controls -when a minister has these wide powers, then that minister surely will not suggest that the name C. D. Howe Company Limited has not some significance beyond that of an ordinary company name.
In any event at a time like this, when in the very nature of things hundreds of millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money are to be spent under the full and unrestrained authority of the Minister of Defence Production, in the preparation of those defence measures which were under discussion in the house yesterday, then there not only should be nothing done which can be open directly to criticism, but there should be nothing done that is open even to indirect criticism, or that gives any colour to the possibility that members of the House of Commons have not reason to repose full confidence in that minister in regard to the expenditure of the enormous sums we are called upon to approve.
Now, the minister himself has stated the relationship of his own family to this company. There is one way in which he could avoid any criticism, and that is to make sure that this company does not retain a name which has a very special significance at this time, and also that no contracts are awarded -and particularly in the circumstances under which these contracts were awarded-in a way that leaves every other contract open to question in so far as that department is concerned.

It is not only government money that is being spent; it is hundreds of millions, billions, of dollars that axe being spent by private companies that must look to the Minister of Defence Production for priority and otherwise. Now, there is no member in this House of Commons who does not know that a nod to any of those private companies, in regard to a company that bears the name of the minister with these immense powers, would be most suggestive and decisive as to what should be done.
It is not necessary to do more than point this out, and to ask the Prime Minister to end the possibility of anything of this kind and to accept these rigid but unwritten rules of obligation and prudence which have been so deeply embedded in our tradition. Unless that is done, then there is only one thing to be said, and that is that from a guilty conscience the charge of "smear" is being made by those whose shameless behaviour opens them to condemnation from every part of this country.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO DEFERMENT OF DEPRECIATION FOR INCOME TAX PURPOSES

speechtext:
Righf Hon. C. D. Howe (Minisler of Defence Production): I table herewith order in council P.C. 3237, dated June 26, amending the regulations relating to deferred capital cost allowances.
Before explaining the changes that have been made in the regulations it may be useful for me to give a short summary of experience under the deferred depreciation plan since it was announced in the budget on April 10.
Between April 11 and June 19, 1951, 257 applications for certificates granting exemption from deferment have been received. Of these 63 have been approved, involving capital expenditures of $12-4 million. Certificates of eligibility granted fall into two groups. One group has been approved under subsection 5 of section 1107 of the income tax regulations, on the ground that they were necessary for the execution of a defence contract or subcontract or were for a purpose which contributed to the defence of Canada. Certificates approved under this section numbered 14, involving capital expenditures of $3-9 million. The second group of certificates granted was under subsection 6 of section 1107 of the income tax regulations. These certificates were approved for capital expenditures required by certain basic industries listed in the regulations for the carrying on of their business. A total number of 49 applications were approved, involving capital outlay of $8-5 million. Certificates have been denied for 26 applications involving $3-4 million. The remaining 168 applications are pending, and these include many applications which will probably qualify for the issuance of a certificate under the regulations as amended.
There is no direct way of measuring the results of the plan. We know how many applications have been received, how many certificates have been issued, and how many have been denied. What we do not know is how many plans have been changed because the businessman knew that depreciation would be deferred for four years. I should point out that the authority to grant certificates for current depreciation is limited, and that many contemplated transactions could not possibly qualify. From information available to the government from various lines of business I think it is fair to say that while the

results cannot be measured precisely, they are substantial. The government believes that the plan has contributed in some measure to the recent reduction of inflationary pressures. It has been a useful supplement to other fiscal and monetary measures and credit restrictions.
On February 8, 1951, I advised the house that our surveys showed investment plans of a record total of $4-3 billion for 1951, or a thirteen per cent increase over the $3-8 billion estimated to have been spent in 1950. The investment plans of business and others have now been resurveyed.
Briefly, the mid-year survey of investment intentions suggests that capital outlays contemplated for 1951 as a whole, including actual expenditures made during the early part of the year, may exceed $4-5 billion. This is five per cent higher than anticipated at the beginning of the year, and twenty per cent above 1950. The increase in capital plans as indicated at mid-year over what appeared to be the outlook at the beginning of the year is almost entirely due to higher purchases of machinery and equipment contemplated mainly by industries either directly or indirectly associated with the defence effort. Such industries include principally those engaged in the production of strategic raw materials and large sectors of manufacturing. In construction little change is indicated, even though the amount of new construction work planned for 1951 is $2-7 billion, or about sixteen per cent above 1950.
While the greater emphasis on investment in defence and defence supporting industries is a change in the right direction, the record capital expenditure program contemplated for 1951 emphasizes the importance of businessmen reviewing carefully their investment plans at the present time and postponing all projects that can, in the judgment of industry, be deferred to a later date.
I turn now to the amendments which have been made in the regulations. These are of five kinds:
1.	Exempting properties acquired by inheritance.
2.	Exempting property depreciable when the order first became effective which is later transferred to a related person or corporation; for example, by incorporation of a sole proprietor or partnership.
3.	Making technical changes in the wording of the order, that is, clarifying the description of certain eligible basic industries.
4.	Adding to the eligible list of basic industries those producing basic chemicals, and filaments, fibres and yarns.
5.	Making the purchase of an existing business, including all the depreciable property,
Capital Cost Allowances eligible for a certificate for current depreciation if the assets involved were depreciable property of the vendor on April 10, 1951.
A number of representations have been made that deferment should not apply to properties which were in existence on April 10 and which merely change hands. The problem is exceedingly complex because of the ease with which such a change if it were adopted could be used to circumvent the purpose of the regulations. The further away we move from April 10, 1951, the more difficult the problem would become. Nevertheless there are certain cases which can, the government believes, be handled.
The amendments exempt from deferment properties acquired by bequest or inheritance and those acquired when the taxpayer and the vendor are not dealing at arm's length, that is, mergers, incorporation of partnerships, incorporation of sole proprietorships, etc. This amendment removes one of the main causes of complaint.
In addition, the purchaser of a business, if he acquires all the depreciable property of the business, may apply to the Minister of Trade and Commerce for a certificate entitling him to exemption from deferment. This certificate will relate only to properties which were used by the vendor in his business and were depreciable property of the vendor on April 10, 1951.
The other amendments are of a more technical nature and are in the main selfexplanatory. The principal changes are those extending the list of industries for which certificates may be issued to include the production of basic chemicals for use in primary industry and the production of filament, fibres or yarns. The principle underlying these changes is consistent with the original intent of the order which was to restrict the list in the main to basic industries which provide the materials for fabrication or which provide transportation or power or some vital utility.
There is another phase of the deferred capital cost allowance provisions which several hon. members have raised here in the house and on which the government has received a number of representations. I am referring to capital expenditure commitments made or projects started before April 11, 1951.
The government is not yet in a position to reach a definite decision on this point. Where genuine commitments were made before April 10, 1951, and must be proceeded with a good case for relief can be made. Mr. Cold well: Last evening, Mr. Chairman, I began to discuss a matter which I said would not take me long, but I acceded to the request of the Minister of Public Works to defer any further mention of it until this morning. Hansard indicates that last night I was speaking of wastage by the armed forces. I said that my attention had been drawn particularly and recently to the loss of a couple of aircraft in the Northwest Territories and in Saskatchewan. Both were Canso planes. One came down in the Northwest Territories on Spitfire lake, about one hundred miles north of Goldfields. When this incident was reported to the government of Saskatchewan, which is extremely anxious to obtain this type of plane because they are excellent for carrying supplies into the far north-I am informed that the plane will carry about four tons of freight-they sent up a pilot and a competent engineer to see if

this plane could be brought back, reconditioned and utilized. When they looked over the situation they found that the engine had been removed and that the plane had been destroyed by fire and, from all appearances, hacked to pieces with axes.
The other similar case was on Ennadai lake, about one hundred miles north of Wollaston lake in the province of Saskatchewan, and the same sort of report was received. This procedure fits in, of course, with what was done after the last war, when a great deal of the equipment was mutilated and destroyed. Indeed, if I may just speak on another branch of the minister's department, it is said that in Saskatoon tires that are taken off army vehicles after they have run a certain distance are destroyed when they could be reconditioned or sold to civilians for farm use. I am reminded that, in connection with the same city, early in the war, I brought to the government's attention or to the attention of the minister of munitions and supply, as the present Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) was then, the matter of the wastage of oil. After some considerable time the minister authorized that the oil might be reconditioned and sold locally for tractors, and so on.
I think that wastage of this description is something that the department should check. We are spending hundreds of millions of dollars for defence supplies with respect to the navy, army and air force; and, as a friend of mine said to me a few days ago, it seems to me that sometimes military men have the idea that army supplies running into millions of dollars can be requisitioned without much question. A careful check should be made on the manner in which supplies are destroyed as unusable when, in my op'inion, in many instances, they could be used. In this particular instance I am of the opinion-as are others, including competent engineers-that the aircraft could have been salvaged, reconditioned and used for the carrying of supplies through northern Canada.
I bring this to the attention of the minister. I mentioned it to him before, and I have no doubt that he has made some inquiries about it. I shall be very glad to hear the results of the inquiry, and to receive, as I know the committee will wish to receive, assurances that instructions have been given that in the event of such occurrences every attempt will be made to salvage rather than to destroy navy, army, and air force equipment.

With regard to the suggestion that tires were destroyed, this charge had been made on a good many occasions back as far as 1941. I remember them long before I had this portfolio. The Minister of Trade and Commerce and of Defence Production is responsible for the procurement of tires, and also for the disposal of tires that have ceased to be
Supply-National Defence serviceable. He assures me that he knows of no case where tires were destroyed. Certainly I have heard of none during the last four and a half years that I have been in this position. All tires that can be made serviceable again are recapped. We even build up the walls of tires. That is done at all the main R.C.E.M.E. depots of the army, and also in the air force and navy. I have watched this operation, and looked into its cost, and I believe it compares very favourably with the cost of any civilian operation, and that we get as big a use out of our tires as any commercial operations.

I should like to bring to the attention of the minister an incident that occurred in March of this year. A number of small fishing craft out from the port of Port Maitland were on a fishing operation five miles off shore when a large ice floe enveloped them. They were unable to reach shore, and had to spend the night out on the ice floe. On the following day three of these craft were able to get to shore. The remaining four were still enveloped in this ice floe. The situation was desperate. There was no way of getting food supplies or fuel to them. A telephone call was put through to the life-saving station at Buffalo to send a helicopter to the rescue. That was the only thing that could drop supplies. These people were trapped in the ice floe three days before a rescue was effected. Food supplies and fuel were dropped, as I say, and if this had not been done they would not have been able to reach shore safely. The situation was indeed desperate.
We in that section of the country were deeply grateful for those services that were provided by the life-saving service of Buffalo. I believe there is an international arrangement between Canada and the United States-

Mr. Speaker, when we last discussed the estimates of the Department of Public Works the hon. member for Calgary East asked me a question about the estimated cost of the printing bureau at Hull. He had put a question on the order paper, and we had answered it to the effect that the original estimate was $11,300,000, and that the actual estimate was $11,300,000. He thought these two figures did not agree because there was an interval of time of two or three years between the two estimates.
I find he was right. I have had a memorandum prepared by the officers of the department, and they say that in 1946, when it was decided to look into the question of relocating and rebuilding the printing bureau, it was considered then that to replace the facilities in the present printing bureau and to expand them to the point where they would meet the requirements of today, an expenditure in the neighbourhood of between $8,000,000 and $10,000,000 would be required.
In the next year, 1947, we had come to the conclusion that the job was of such magnitude that the best interests of the public would be served by our engaging an industrial engineer, experienced in the construction of public printing plants. We accordingly made arrangement with Mr. M. E. Powers, of Chicago, who made a trip to Ottawa, and we worked with him and the king's printer in an endeavour to
4824

Supply-Public Works determine primarily the facilities to be provided, and, secondly, the size and type of building required to have them operate in the most economical way.
Two years later, in 1949, after we had studied the problem and determined the size of the building, we engaged the services of a Montreal architect to prepare detailed plans and specifications. In April, 1949, we received a preliminary estimate from him of $9,293,818. This estimate has been revised since 1949, and on May 1, 1951, the estimate given by our architect is $11,300,000.

I should like to thank the minister for that statement, because it clears up some of the points I questioned before.
There are two other points. I asked what the present estimate of the total cost would be, and I got the figure of $11,300,000. Then I asked what the present estimated total cost of the building would be. The answer was, "Answered by No. 1". speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
When the building is constructed there will be no flooding. This spring the creek which runs behind the site overflowed, and as the work was not advanced the water went into the excavation which was referred to by certain newspapers as a lake. They brought in a rowboat when they took a picture of the site. When the building is completed there will be no flooding. The water that did come in had to be taken out by the contractor.
In answer to the second question I am told that the cost of the site is included in the $11,300,000.

The returns state that the cost of the building is $11,300,000, and therefore I would take it that that includes the cost of the site. The minister says there will be no flooding, but I would think there will be considerable expense in diking or filling in the land so that the property will not be flooded. This water was not only in the excavation; it covered the surrounding land, and there will have to be some kind of antiflood protection provided in the way of dikes or filling to make the land higher.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am told that no diking will be required once the building is completed. If the water should come up to the building there would be no flooding because it is built on solid rock.

I still am not too clear on this matter. Does the minister now say that the return was incorrect, and that the figure of
IMr. Fournier (Hull).]

$11,300,000, which- was given as the present estimated cosit, is not the cost of the building?

I would not say that there was a mistake in the answer, but there was certainly a misunderstanding. We never take as the final estimate guesses made in 1946, or preliminary estimates made in 1946 and 1949. The final figure which I considered at the time as the real estimate is $11,300,000. There may be a misunderstanding as to the next part. I am told by my officials that the cost of the site is included in that amount of $11,300,000.
It is getting a little late in the session to pursue this any further, so I shall leave it until next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

would like to have public buildings in their constituencies, and I would not raise this question now if I had not brought it to the attention of the minister on previous occasions. While I am asking the minister that question may I point out that there is a decrease of a million and three-quarters in the appropriation for public works in Alberta this year. I notice, of course, that there is a decrease in almost every province; but the largest decrease, except that in Quebec, is in Alberta. That may be a good sign; it may mean that Alberta has a good government, but it does seem to me that one or two more projects that may be necessary in Alberta might have been proceeded with. In fairness to the minister I should point out that the summary for his department shows a decrease of $18,721,310, which is commendable in these days when we want to cut our expenditures a little.

speechtext:
The hon. member is

Where is it to be built?

That will be right in town, will it?

I want to commend the government on their action in this regard. It is long overdue.

I should like to ask one
question in this connection; possibly the answer is in the supplementary estimates, but I am not sure. There is an item of $1 in the supplementaries for Fraser Valley, and that is probably my answer. Will the property be acquired and construction of the building commenced?

which should be asked) on1 the supplementary estimates, but I have no objection to answering it now. Is that just for Huntingdon or the Fraser Valley riding? Is that dollar for the whole of British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
If you look at page
38 of the supplementary estimates you will see that we cover Abbotsford and Huntingdon, buildings for customs and immigration. Supply-Public Works

I notice, Mr. Chairman, that there are a couple of items in the British Columbia appropriation for customs and immigration buildings. I might point out to the minister what I believe is a general feeling among our people in respect to the public buildings at various ports of entry into Canada along the United States boundary. I have had to cross into the United States and back into Canada on a number of occasions and at a number of different places. I urge the minister to do what he can for the improvement of our buildings at these ports of entry, because when we compare these buildings with the ones on the United States side of the line there appears to be quite a difference. There are just as many people going one way as coming the other, I fancy, unless there are settlers who are coming here to stay.
First impressions are very important. I am afraid that quite often our friends from the United States receive an unfavourable first impression. They pass their own public buildings, and then come to ours. Some of them are just not in the same class at all. The impression they immediately receive is that we are not so up and coming as they are; we are a poor country compared with their country. That is not so, because we are a wealthy country. I am going to suggest that the minister do what he can or what the government will permit him to do along that line. It may be a fancy of mine, but even the immigration and customs officials do not seem to be as well dressed as the United States officials. I hope that is not regarded as a harsh criticism, but to me, and I believe to many others, all these things are important.

I should like to come back to Huntingdon. If my memory serves me correctly, an item of $200,000 was placed in the estimates for that building, and voted. I appreciate the shortage of steel, though sometimes when I hear from my motorcar dealers who are endeavouring to sell cars that are stacked a mile wide and a mile high in British Columbia, I do not think there is a shortage of steel. I see $250,000 voted for Osoyoos, which is in the riding of the member for Yale. I have no objection to Osoyoos securing a customs and immigration building. I happen to know Osoyoos probably as well as the average member in this house. With one good hop and a jump one could drive right over the place. I do not customarily boast about the Fraser valley. The records will show what the traffic is both from the customs point of view and from the immigration point of view through Osoyoos and through Huntingdon, and there is no comparison whatsoever. I do not need to say that the records of the Department of

supply-Public Works National Revenue will show that. I do not want to blame the minister and his department unfairly. For that reason I should like him to tell me on whose recommendation $250,000 was put in the estimates this year to build a customs building at Osoyoos, when Huntingdon, the second port-
Carried.

You know, Mr. Chairman, some of my good friends in that minority group over on the opposite side of the chamber, between eight and nine o'clock, sometimes take a little bit of extra time by saying "carried, carried". But when one represents the second largest port of entry in British Columbia, he is entitled to know why there is no item in the estimates this year for Huntingdon. If it is a shortage of material, all right; I can appreciate that difficulty and I believe my people can understand it. But we cannot understand a shortage of material at Huntingdon and no shortage at Osoyoos. We cannot understand $250,000 for a building at a small port of entry when there is no item to construct a building at Huntingdon. I should like to know from the minister, through you, Mr. Chairman, the reason for that and if it is going to be sidetracked definitely or if it is going to be carried through. In this case, for once at least, I can be substantiated by records of the Department of National Revenue-I could not be substantiated particularly on my own income tax, but I can in this case-that the entry from the main city of Seattle in the state of Washington is through this district. Why has it been overlooked?
Carried.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Just a minute. I think I owe the hon. member an explanation. As to Osoyoos, the contract was given last year. The work is proceeding along, and "this item of $250,000 is to complete the work. At Huntingdon, the site has not been purchased and the plans have not been prepared. That is why I have an item in the supplementary estimates

so there would be no feud between those two places. We have a supplementary estimate for the purchase of the site and the preparation of the plans. A building started last year would be advanced to such a point that we would have to complete it. As to a building not started yet, I am held back by lack of materials. But my hon. friend knows that he can rely on me, on my good will, and my good intentions.

I have just one word to say. The Minister of Public Works is probably the fairest man in this committee, with the possible exception of the hon. member for Fraser Valley. I know that he will do the

right thing for my riding. As I understand it, an estimate will be put in next year for some $500,000 for Huntingdon.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, I would not make that promise.

Well, between $400,000 and $500,000. I want to make this suggestion to the minister now, as a result of the experience in my riding which has been fairly treated by the minister's department. I want to suggest to him that, before plans are prepared for the new building, his architect or whoever is responsible for this work should visit our particular district and size up this particular building. The reason I am emphasizing that point, Mr. Chairman, is this. We have had three new post offices built. As I say, the department have been extremely fair in my riding. We had three new post offices built. We have a basement in there big enough for a bowling alley but which is of no use at all. That sort of thing may be all right in eastern Canada. It is the taxpayers' money that is going to pay for these benefits in my riding; and I am merely suggesting that the department either have a British Columbia architect prepare the plans or that they give me the assurance that the local architect will view the site prior to the preparation of the plans, and prepare their plans according to the needs of western Canada, not along the lines of what may be necessary in eastern Canada. As I stated, two buildings were built within two years. They built fine buildings. But thousands of dollars have been spent on basements which are unnecessary and are unused in our province. I should like the assurance of the minister that the matter to which I have referred will be given consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh yes; I certainly will consider the remarks made by the hon. gentleman.
No basements in Fraser valley.

I should like to draw to the attention of the Minister of Public Works the fact that, in most cases where these post offices are not being built, he has used the same excuse for their not being built, namely that there is a shortage of steel.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.

I was wondering whether the steel companies are brushing him off in that way. I notice that one post office is being built-in fact there are a couple-and that there was no shortage of steel for them; and those post offices had not been promised as had other ones. For instance, I referred to the new post office being built in Montreal, on Windsor street. It is to take a whole block there from St. James up to St. Antoine.

There is no scarcity of steel there. It is a big building, having seven storeys or perhaps more. I see that they have been allowed steel, and we did not hear anything about that post office as we did about the others three and four years ago; yet the shortage of steel exists with regard to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In all fairness to my department, may I say that the building mentioned by the hon. gentleman was started two years ago. The steel was ordered two years ago. I do not know whether it is near completion or not. It has been on the way. I can tell the hon. member that two months ago I still had trouble with regard to the steel for that building. Actually I had contracts ready to be finalized, but the contractors hesitated to take the contract because I could not give them any assurance that they will get the steel. I have no control over the steel. That is the real reason.
You had no difficulty in getting that steel for that big building.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is two years ago.

353. Salaries, surveys, inspections, test borings, etc., $1,588,512.

I hope I am speaking on the right item. I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works to something that exists along the Ottawa river which I think is detrimental to many of the people using the river. I refer to the fact that every Saturday the water in the Ottawa river below Des Joachims is lower by at least 18 inches than on Monday morning.
I think that is due to the controlling of the water at the hydro project at Des Joachims, or possibly our own dam at Timiskaming. It is quite costly to many of the lumber companies and others who use the river, as well as the men who transport us across the river at Pembroke and Allumette Island. Can something be done in regard to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, that does come under my department. We have employees at the Timiskaming dam which regulates the flow of the water according to the demand for power. On Sunday when they close it the water rises in the headrace and decreases in the tailrace. This man has been on the job for years, and I am told that he knows his work quite well. He is doing his best so that people will not suffer because of the difference in the level of the water. We cannot keep it at the same level always, but we try.

I think that possibly the hydro dam at Des Joachims is the cause of the lowering of the water. There must be some agreement in respect to that dam. I think the trouble is with the dam at Des Joachims. They are not regulating water as they should.

Supply-Public Works

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am told that we have something to do with the hydro dam. This is the first year of operation of this new dam, and we are trying to find the real level that will satisfy everybody in that part of the country.

What is being done at the present time in regard to this interprovincial bridge? I know that steel is one of the reasons delaying construction at the present time. Are we getting an agreement with the provinces so that we can go ahead with this bridge when steel is available? The people of Pontiac and the people of north Renfrew feel that we should get this bridge as soon as possible. There is one thing that I should like to tell the committee. speechtext: I believe this is one of the projects that we are committed to, and we will proceed with it as soon as circumstances permit the obtaining of the material. This is a resume of the letters that we received from Mr. Frost and Mr. Duplessis, and I think they are binding on the different parties. We will certainly proceed with this bridge the moment that we can have the materials.
Has any plan been prepared for this bridge? I understand that Quebec maintains that they are not able to get the necessary information that they wish to have.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

I have one question I would like to ask. I do not expect the minister to have all the answers at his fingertips. With respect to the trans-Canada highway, in British Columbia we have a portion of the route between Fry's corner and King George highway. This highway is a main part of the trans-Canada highway within our province. It was built many years ago and is totally inadequate under present conditions.
I notice by the press that the minister's department has informed the provincial government that they are not prepared to reconstruct this portion of the trans-Canada highway, owing to the fact that it requires


paving and, under modern conditions, hard surfacing. This particular portion of the highway serves not only the district that I happen to represent but the entire lower mainland of British Columbia.
That part of the trans-Canada highway was constructed prior to modern road building. Because it affects that forgotten district of Vancouver island to Victoria all the tourists coming into that part of the country-in Victoria our slogan is "Follow the birds"- have to come over this highway.
I am perfectly satisfied to accept any of the minister's decisions as to the amount of traffic on the highway, but what I am particularly concerned about is this. According to press reports the minister's department has said that this must lie in abeyance until normal conditions return. This is the main part of the highway entering into the city of Vancouver; it is a main part of the trans-Canada highway. It is the route adopted by the provincial government and by the federal government, I understand, leading into Vancouver across the Pattullo bridge. I am referring particularly to that part between Fry's corner and the King George highway. Is the minister's department prepared or willing to pay the federal share now for the construction of that piece of the trans-Canada highway according to the qualifications laid down?

To the best of my knowledge we have had no specific application with respect to that portion of the highway. Under the terms of the agreement the federal government contributes 50 per cent of the cost incurred by the provincial government. Where the highway is within a municipality, the normal arrangement exists for payment of that portion of the cost normally incurred by the municipality, and then the federal government shares the provincial government's cost on the 50-50 basis, under the terms of the agreement.

That brings in something new. Am I given to understand that a municipality is called upon to bear their share of the cost of the trans-Canada highway within that municipality? I want this to be particularly clear because I do not think the people of British Columbia understood it that way. Are we as a municipality called upon to bear a share of the costs of the trans-Canada highway in conjunction with the provincial and federal authorities?

That is a matter to be determined between the provincial government and the municipality. The federal government undertakes to pay half the cost incurred by the provincial government. If in the

normal arrangement the municipality is required to contribute toward the cost of roads, then that is something between the municipality and the province.
I think that is bringing something new into the trans-Canada highway as I understand it.

No. If I may answer that I can read the section from the trans-Canada highway agreement. It is section 3 (5) and reads as follows:
If the provincial practice has been to assist the municipality financially in the construction of its highways cr bridges and proposes to follow this practice in regard to the trans-Canada highway, the federal contribution will be considered to an amount not greater than one-half the contribution made by the province. The province, however, must give prior advice to the federal authorities of its intentions in this respect.

The minister has
explained the situation.. Constructing highways in my province is entirely different from constructing highways in the prairie provinces, for example. In the prairie provinces they can construct 20 miles of highway at the same price that it would cost us in British Columbia to construct half a mile. That is known to everyone. As it was explained by the minister I understood that the municipalities would not be called upon to contribute in any way. I wish to make it clear that I did not think they were to contribute to the trans-Canada highway.
The section to which I am referring leads into the third city of Canada. After all, that third city of Canada is entitled to some consideration. From the monetary point of view, the influx of American dollars through the great port of Vancouver means something to the foreign exchange situation in this country. The impression I was given from press reports, rightly or wrongly, was to the effect that the federal government had said that it would not contribute at this time to the rebuilding of any highway. Let me make it clear that that was stated in the press of British Columbia, particularly Vancouver- that the federal government would not contribute to the rebuilding of any highway that called for pavement or hard-surfacing. I believe one of those expressions was used.
To my mind that is a serious statement. I had not intended before to say anything, but I think now I shall have something to say about the matter. I want to have that point cleared up for the constituency of Fraser Valley particularly the municipalities of Chilliwack, Sumas and Matsqui. Are the taxpayers of those municipalities to be asked in any shape or form to contribute to the cost of the construction or reconstruction of the trans-Canada highway?

question.

I appreciate what the
minister has said, that we will have to contribute our normal share, whatever the percentage is. But that is certainly new to me. When I first heard about the trans-Canada highway I had no idea-and I do not think the people throughout the province had any idea-that at the will or whim of the provincial government the individual municipalities could be called upon to contribute a share of the costs of the trans-Canada highway. I wish the minister would get more authentic and more definite information.

Well, I do not come from the maritime provinces. I come from that great province of British Columbia, where the tourists go. Hon. members may call "carried" all they like; but in my riding the municipalities are not going to be called upon to pay any share of the trans-Canada highway until we have a better definition than has been given to me thus far. I would ask the minister to explain a little more fully.
I know he wants to do the right thing and that the government wants to do the right thing. I believe the provincial governments want to do the right thing. But in my province we have the privilege of saying that we come from the old state of Missouri, from which the president of the United States comes-and I am referring to that old expression, that we are from Missouri. Will the municipalities of Chilliwack, Sumas and Matsqui be called upon to contribute any share toward the cost of the trans-Canada highway?
Before the item carries-
Just a minute; I asked a question.

I repeat that the federal government's agreement is with the provincial governments. I read the section from the

Supply-Resources and Development agreement which covers that particular phase of the operation. I think that is clear. I do not think there is any misunderstanding in the interpretation. My hon. friend may not like the interpretation, but that is a quite different matter. We have undertaken to pay one-half of the cost incurred by the provincial governments. I am sure the government in British Columbia, as well as other governments in the various provinces, will deal fairly with their municipalities. While I do not know whether the municipalities to which my hon. friend referred will be required to pay, I do know that the policy followed by the government of British Columbia is a fair one. I think he can be assured that his municipalities will receive fair consideration.

I know that, so far as the minister is concerned, we will receive fair consideration. I must say however that I did not understand when the act was passed to build the trans-Canada highway that the provinces were to assess the municipalities. I speak for the people I represent. I believe such a procedure would be a very dangerous thing and should not be permitted. It is within the jurisdiction of the provinces to tax or not to tax local landlords.
In other words all hon. members know that a sidewalk or street lights may be placed [DOT]on Sparks street here in Ottawa and benefit the property owners on that street. But to permit the province to tax the taxpayers in a rural municipality is not fair. It may be different out in the middle of Saskatchewan, although I do not think they are very prosperous out there. I do not think the province should assess through the municipal authorities to pay a share of the cost, in conjunction with the provincial and federal authorities. My understanding was that the trans-Canada highway was to be built by the federal and provincial authorities. I did not understand that it involved municipal taxation.
I happen to own a farm. To be frank about it, I have heard something about personal interests entering into things-which they should not, I know. But is my farm to be taxed so as to build the trans-Canada highway through it?
Well, Mr. Chairman, pressure has been brought to bear upon me, and I have confidence enough in the federal minister that it will not be permitted. I have not equal confidence in the ministerial authority within my own province. I have registered my objection and I can say nothing more. All this appeared in the press, including the Vancouver press. It was stated that the federal government would not let them build this section of highway because it was really

a repaving project. The minister can shake his head, but that was in the press where the people of British Columbia could read it. I do not believe everything I read in the press, but I do want to make sure that the people of my riding are protected, not against the press who have always been fair, but against other people who have not been so fair.

I agree with the hon.
member for Fraser Valley that no municipality should have to pay the cost of a trunk highway going through its town. I know this is a provincial matter, as the minister has pointed out, but I submit there should be something in the act to stop the provincial government charging any part of its share of fifty per cent of the cost to any municipality. I am absolutely against this and I have always been against it. I do not think any small municipality or town should have to bear any part of the cost of a trunk highway going through that municipality or town. Very little has been done in New Brunswick with regard to the trans-Canada highway. As our trunk roads are in bad condition I should like to ask if anything is to be done this year.
I understand that the provincial government of New Brunswick intends to go ahead this year with some of the work on the trans-Canada highway.

Has there been any change
in the route through New Brunswick? I do not agree with the present route up the Saint John river valley because within forty miles there are fourteen railroad crossings which could have been eliminated by going up the opposite side of the river.

I am somewhat in agreement with the hon. member who has just taken his seat when he says that we are not making much progress with the construction of this highway. I refer particularly to the new sections, particularly in Ontario, not to sections that are being reconstructed. I was interested in the remarks of the minister about the road from Sudbury to Chapleau being designated as the trans-Canada highway. There was a great deal of talk that the trans-Canada highway would run from Sudbury to Sault Ste. Marie and then north to Port Arthur.	,

It runs from Sudbury to
Chapleau via Thessalon, which is in the general direction of Sault Ste. Marie.

Those of us who have
travelled the road between Sudbury and Sault Ste. Marie know that there has been a great deal of construction on this section. I

think it would have been possible for them to have completed the road from Sudbury to Sault Ste. Marie this year and progress could have been made in building north to Port Arthur. I think the whole section could be completed within a short time. It does not make much difference how rapidly the other provinces complete their sections of the trans-Canada highway if the section north of the great lakes is not completed. We are losing millions of dollars in tourist trade every year because the road north of the great lakes is not completed. My judgment is that that section is not being built as rapidly as it could be.
I believe the federal government should take steps to see that a province builds so many miles of new trans-Canada highway each year before it qualifies for the grant. By the time the agreement has expired there is bound to be a lot of the highway not completed. Most of the provinces in western Canada will have their sections completed within two or three years at the most, but I venture to predict that the section north of the great lakes in Ontario will not be completed.
The progress made on the new sections of the trans-Canada highway has not been too rapid within the last two or three years. I should like to see the minister get after the department in Ontario that has jurisdiction over the trans-Canada highway and put on a little pressure in an effort to have this section completed. It would be of benefit in increased tourist business as well as from the military point of view. It would enable Canadian citizens going to western Canada to travel an all-Canadian route instead of having to go down through the United States.
I take it that there is no objection to the federal government reconstructing the trans-Canada highway between the King George highway and Fry's corner?
We have not had representations from the provincial government with respect to that particular section and we would not make a decision until such representations are received.
I presume there would be no objection to the federal government hard-surfacing the trans-Canada highway?
We propose to carry out the terms of our agreement and I think the province will find us pretty easy to get along with.

Has there been a slowing down of work on the trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland, and has that been done at the suggestion of the Minister of Finance?

As a matter of general policy the federal government has asked the provincial governments-it has taken the same attitude with its own operations-to go forward only with those projects which they consider essential. Of course we have no control over the provincial governments and would not attempt to influence them in any way. We let it be known that that was the policy we were adopting, but at the same time we told the provincial governments that, if they attached a high order of importance to the trans-Canada highway and considered it to be essential to the development of their economy, they would find us willing to co-operate. I know of no slowing down in Newfoundland.

The premier made the statement that he was deliberately slowing down the work at the suggestion of the Minister of Finance. The minister knows very well that this is an extremely important matter to the province and I do hope something will be done by the minister to try to have the premier change his attitude. It is going to be unfortunate if we have to keep on waiting for a road across the island. I think we are safe now in saying there is no necessity for slowing down this work, that it is purely the decision of the premier if he wishes to do so. Is that the situation?

Well, it is up to the provincial governments to evaluate the importance of this work. I think I should say to the hon. member that in point of work committed Newfoundland stands fourth among the eight provinces participating in this agreement.
That is in work completed?
No; in work committed.
That is for this year?
Since the agreement was entered into.
That is the work that has been done, not the new work coming up. Is not the minister aware that the premier has decided not to go ahead? Has he not told you that?
I have not seen the statement the hon. member attributes to the premier of Newfoundland.

I agree with the remarks as to the building of the road through northern Ontario north of the great lakes; but I cannot agree with the route further along, as I did not agree at the time the original route was being mapped out. At that time I pointed out to the minister and others that the highway would be blocked by snow during the winter. Recent storms have proved me right. Apparently it is going to be blocked by snow in the month of June as well. The hon. member for Medicine Hat, the hon. member for Bow River and all the others along that southern route should now admit they were wrong and the government was wrong in following their suggestion to have the highway go through the southern part of the provinces. I am going to suggest now that if that route is still to be followed work should commence immediately on another highway following the Yellowhead route from Winnipeg west to Edmonton. I believe the present defence program demands that this be done. I hope the minister will take very serious notice of this and act accordingly.

I had no intention of getting into this argument until the hon. member for Battle River had his say. We must agree that he tried to have the highway follow the northern route, but I believe the dominion and provincial governments were very wise in putting the trans-Canada highway where they did. If it went through the northern part of the province United States tourists would never get up there. So I am very happy that the road is to go through Medicine Hat.

I think I would be remiss in my duty if I did not urge the minister to reconsider, with the province, the route designated for the highway north of the great lakes. My riding includes Sault Ste. Marie, which is the gateway used by forty million tourists from the south. If this highway were to go north of Sault Ste. Marie, up around the north shore of lake Superior, I am sure the revenue from the tourist trade alone would more than pay for the construction of the road. Sault Ste. Marie is the only port of entry between Sarnia on the south and the Manitoba boundary on the west. Once more I urge the minister to reconsider if at all possible the route that has been chosen, and have this highway follow the shore north of lake Superior. At present the road is built some eighty miles north of Sault Ste. Marie, and should be continued. While the country I mentioned is rugged, that is one of the main reasons for urging that the road be taken through it, because the ruggedness of the country does attract tourists from the United States.

Has the federal government supervision over this trans-Canada highway, or are they going to let the provinces build it as they please? Who is to have supervision, the provinces or the federal government?

We are both giving supervision. The provinces are building the road to standards which were mutually agreed upon and which are laid down in the agreement. They have their engineers on the road, and we have our engineers to see that the standards jointly agreed to are maintained.
Are some of the provinces going to be allowed to put off old highways on the federal government to make up their fifty per cent?
No, sir, they will not.
I understand that is what is being done in New Brunswick.

Forest conservation and wildlife management, including Wood Buffalo park-

I would like to ask a question concerning wildlife services. I do not know whether this was brought up on the national parks estimates or on any previous occasion, but I would like to know what is being done by this department, if anything, in connection with predator control. I mention this because of the serious damage that is done to our game animals iby the predators, particularly wolves. As I mentioned' before, these wolves are protected in the national parks; they increase rapidly; they form gangs or packs of killers, and do enormous damage both inside and outside the parks. I had hoped the policy of the department would be altered so that wolves and certain other predators could be shot within the national parks, but that has not been done. It has been decided by those in charge of national parks and by others, that in order to preserve their game, predator control is one of the most important measures they can take. Predators do infinitely more damage to game, animals than overshooting or overhunting. I do not know whether this question has been brought up before, but if it has I apologize. I did not hear it. If it has not, will the minister make a statement?

The matter has not been brought up this year, but it was brought up last year. I well remember the hon. member referring to it in an interesting way when the estimates were before the house. The problem, which receives a great deal of attention from that branch of the department, is one of trying to maintain a proper balance, which often is a matter of judgment. In the national parks in particular, part of our job is to maintain the park area in its natural state, having regard to (both vegetation and wildlife. We are trying, by various means, to maintain a proper balance. We have provided for the payment of bounties and taken other measures from time to time for the killing of predators as the situation warranted. We take whatever steps seem to be indicated, in

I wish first of all to commend the minister for the program announced earlier in the year in connection with forest conservation. I believe that forest conservation is one of the most important types of conservation of our natural resources. I am sorry that the estimate for this year is down considerably from last year.

Might I raise a point of order to remind my hon. friend that he might more properly discuss that item under vote 416. This vote No. 412 is for forest conservation and wildlife management, including Wood Buffalo park.

Forestry branch-
416. Branch administration, $81,971.

I note that the amount for operation and maintenance is considerably up from last year, which in my opinion is all to the good. I come from a province which, perhaps at this date, is one of the best forested provinces in Canada. But I am quite satisfied that during the past decade we have been losing more by cutting, fires and insects than we are making up by natural growth. This state of affairs cannot continue for very long. So far as we in British Columbia are concerned the depletion of our forests would be a national calamity, because a large amount of our revenue comes from that source. I realize that only a small proportion of forest conservation could, of necessity, come under the jurisdiction of the minister's department. I would urge him to continue trying to get the provinces, particularly those of them that have not realized the dangerous situation confronting us, to put more and more effort into conservation. Then, instead of taking more out of our forests each year than comes back through natural growth, the natural growth will more than meet the depletion.
There is a great deal that could be said on this subject, but I am not going to take up the time of the committee at the moment. The benefits of forest conservation are not limited to the forest, but they extend to the whole economy of our country. I would commend the minister for what he has done, and urge him to approach this subject with real effort and determination.
