419. Forestry operations division, including forest insects control board, $63,858.

Can the minister say if his department is doing anything in regard to
4844	HOUSE OF
Supply-Resources and Development the army worm or tent caterpillar as it is called, which has covered nearly all of Ontario this year, killing trees. I know that oak trees that have been infested with the worm for the last two years have died. Poplar, elm and birch trees are dead from the effects of these worms.
The problem of studying the army worm or tent caterpillar, and insects of that kind, is the responsibility federally of the science service of the Department of Agriculture.

Can the minister say if the Department of Agriculture is doing anything about it? Last year the Minister of Agriculture said that these caterpillars would not kill the trees, but that was wrong because the trees are dead. Surely, one of the departments must be doing something about them. This is the forestry branch, and surely insects must come under that branch. The description of the vote is, "Forestry operations division, including forest insects control board."

This is a vote that was set up to provide for administration of the dominion-provincial operations that I announced earlier in the house under the Canada Forestry Act. But a portion of the vote is for the forest insects control board, and this is a small vote of $3,600 which is for travelling expenses in connection with the operations of that board.
It is not necessary to provide for any travelling expenses for the caterpillars, because they travel under their own power.

As to this matter of insect control, this department is, I would say, responsible for a certain amount of the control of insects, especially the caterpillar and also of the grub that eats or kills the birch in New Brunswick. Because of the fact that great timber areas in the various provinces are close to each other, if one province does something and the other one does not, the action does not have the effect it should have. We should therefore have, coming from the dominion, some control of the tent caterpillar, the birch worm and the sawfly. I think that is the proper place for it to come from because we have a good, young minister who is full of energy. I think he should take this matter up with the provinces and do something that will really produce an effect.
This is an extremely important item, Mr. Chairman. The budworm has killed practically all the birch in the province of New Brunswick.
And it is coming into Quebec and Ontario now.

As my hon. friend says, it is now coming up into Quebec and Ontario. If something is not done, a great Canadian industry will be put out of business. Practically all of the birch mills and the hardwood mills in New Brunswick have been closed down on account of this worm. Something must be done. Instead of this item being lowered, in my opinion it should be increased. We must do something about this problem. This infestation will cover Ontario and Quebec in a few years if it is not stopped.
And it will kill the tourist traffic undoubtedly because there will not be any trees for the tourists in Ontario or in any other part of the country.
As I told my hon. friend earlier, this is a matter that is dealt with by the science service of the Department of Agriculture. We assist them where we can and to the extent that we can.
Will the minister say that he will take the matter up with the Department of Agriculture and see that something is done about it?
I shall be glad to take the matter up with them. I cannot guarantee that something will be done about it, but I will take it up with them.
We should not have the thing tossed around. Somebody has to do something.
They have the vote.

It seems to me that this matter is still left in an unsatisfactory position. I am not undertaking to say what the division of duties is; but we have really a very slight acceptance of responsibility, if indeed any, by the present minister. Yet this is a thing that stares us in the face. It is something for which some minister ought to be made fully responsible now, so that we cannot have it just tossed around from place to place.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I understood the minister
to say that part of this money was for the administration of the forestry act. May I ask whether, under that act which amongst other things provides for research, there has been any research-in recent months or indeed since the act was put through the house- into the question of the part played by tailor-made cigarettes in causing forest fires? As the minister will recall, I raised this matter a number of times. I do not want to repeat the speeches that I made on those occasions, but I still feel that it is a subject concerning

which some useful and valuable research might be done. There is no doubt in my mind that, with regard to our forests, greater danger is created by tailor-made cigarettes than by any other kind. Indeed I believe they are the cause of a great many fires, in our cities as well as in our forests. It seems to me that something might be done with regard to the chemicals, either in the tobacco itself or in the paper, to make sure that the cigarettes do not produce quite so much danger. My question is this. Has there been any research by the branch with regard to this matter?

The department has done no active research in the matter. I well remember my hon. friend raising the subject last year. The cigarette manufacturers are aware of the problem and are trying, by means of advertising, to undertake a program of fire prevention. I am well aware of my hon. friend's representations and I will keep them in mind.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What the minister says is quite correct, namely that since we raised this matter in the house on a number of occasions, the cigarette companies have been spending money on advertising campaigns in the interests of fire prevention. 426. To assist in promoting the tourist business in Canada, $1,503,197.

This deals with the Canadian government travel bureau, and is an item involving over $ 1 .j million. I must say that this is one item of the minister's department that I do not look at with any great degree of satisfaction, and I do not think that any hon. member does. We in this country have a great deal to offer to the tourist. As we all know, this particular part of the present minister's department has been kicked around like a football ever since it was initiated under a former administration. What alarms me, Mr. Chairman, is some of the returns which I have. I say this in view of the increased amount of money spent on the tourist industry in every country that enjoys a tourist industry.
According to the return I received a few days ago, I find that in 1950 the estimated tourist revenue for Canada was $275 million. The other item in the return which also concerns me is the advertising which went to Cockfield Brown advertising agency, namely, $921,925.10. I am putting these figures up against the total revenue in 1948 of $280 million and in 1949 of $288 million. In other words, in 1950 we dropped some $13 million at a time when the tourist industry in the United States, France, Switzerland and elsewhere was very much increased. If I were to look at these figures as a businessman, as I think the minister should, and see what they reflect, I do not think I would hesitate very long before doing something about them.
I have spoken on this subject at great length at different times. I do not intend to take up a great deal of time at this moment discussing it, but I am going to suggest to the minister that he might well consider some of the suggestions that have been made from outside the house in the last four or

five years relative to an increase in this industry. We want United States dollars. We on this continent have more to offer than any other country, and yet our tourist industry is going down instead of up. More money was spent last year on the tourist industry elsewhere than ever before. Our revenue decreased, yet we have greater accommodation available and more roads. I do not think we got our fair share of the tourist dollar that was spent last year. I know that the minister has various branches in his department, but I am saying quite sincerely that we should develop a billion dollar industry in this country and not a $280 million industry. Switzerland gets close to a billion dollars from the tourist industry. It is her main source of revenue, but she has not one-tenth of what we have to offer, nor has she the number of people so close to her borders. We are living next door to more than 150 million people who are vacation-minded, and who would be glad to come to this country.
I want to conclude with this point. When the minister and his department face these figures let them face them with reality and realize that there is something wrong when they cannot produce more revenue in this branch of the department.

When hon. members put questions on the order paper and an order for return is passed, that return should contain the information which is asked for. I placed a question on the order paper, which was passed as an order for return by the house, asking for expenditures of government departments for advertising during the fiscal year 1949-50. When I got the return I found that practically all the departments had given me pretty detailed statements of the amounts expended in advertising. But the Department of Resources and Development was quite conspicuous by its answers to the questions. I found the Department of Resources and Development advertising placed with Cockfield Brown and Company Limited, Montreal, Quebec; and two, the amount, nil. No amounts paid. The answer said that they work on commission from magazines and newspapers in accordance with established agency practice. But obviously the information was available in the department because when I turned up the public accounts and saw how vote 383 of that year was expended on the Canadian government travel bureau I found advertising and publicity. I find that under "advertising and publicity" note A includes payments to Cockfield Brown and Company Limited, Montreal, $910,567.92, and national
Supply-Resources and Development film board, $56,020.25. The total spent for advertising reported altogether was $977,067.15.
It seems to me that when a member of the house puts a motion for a return asking a department to give the expenditure in regard to any estimate, the return should give the information requested. I found it in the public accounts. It seems to me that Cockfield Brown and Company are receiving very large advertising fees from this government, very large commissions therefor for the magazines and periodicals. And when we know who is the representative of Cockfield Brown in this city-the national secretary, I believe, of the Liberal association- it seems to me that they are getting a very large amount of advertising, and that the commission is very considerable.
But what I am objecting to is that when I place a motion for a return showing certain expenditures, the return made in the house indicates nil. Yet when I look up the public accounts I find nearly $1 million given as the expenditure. The house has a right to expect that when it passes an order for return, no matter who moves it, the information will be brought down, and brought down in full; and that we will not have to turn to some other document and find that instead of nil the expenditure is almost $1 million. As I say, this was not the case with the other departments of government. This department was conspicuous because it did not do what the other departments of government did when they were asked to fill in answers by the Secretary of State for the return tabled in the house.
I say that because I think when on another occasion one moves an order for return of this description he is entitled to at least the same information as is provided in the blue book, the public accounts.
While I am on my feet I want to say that with its limited means the travel or tourist bureau is doing a commendable job. I think a better one could be done, and I think it could be better if there were more supervision by the provinces of the accommodation provided tourists when they come to Canada. I think that much of the tourist accommodation outside private homes is rather primitive. Americans who come to Canada go back with a very bad impression of our sanitary arrangements, and very often a bad impression of the general conditions of tourist accommodation.
It used to be that in some provinces our roads were a barrier to bringing tourists to the country; but to a large extent that is no longer true. Some of the roads into this country from the south are now equal to

Supply-Resources and Development anything they have in the United States. I am glad to say that in the last six years my own province of Saskatchewan has done a tremendous job in that respect. But today it is tourist accommodation that is required, and I think that in respect of both living accommodation and the provision of food the department could do a great deal to encourage the provinces-and here I blame the provinces to some extent-to give closer supervision to the type of tourist accommodation offered, and particularly the sanitary conveniences and arrangements in connection with those places.
Today people will not come to this country unless they can get something comparable to that which they are able to get in their own country. I said "something comparable"; I do not mean that in a country like this, with our great distances and our smaller population, we can give them altogether the type of accommodation they get in the United States. But I think if the department brought more pressure to bear on the provincial authorities to see that at least sanitary arrangements were better, it would help our tourist business considerably.
I think, too, that a great deal more could be done by way of advertising Canada in the United States. I am not offering any suggestions, but the amounts we allow the tourist bureau are not large. I hope more can be done to encourage people to come and see this very magnificent country. I know that a great deal of country has been opened up in Ontario, Nova Scotia, the maritime provinces, British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, where there is beautiful scenery, splendid fishing and hunting, and all the rest of it.

When you step into the city of Quebec you step into old France; and that has charm for tourists which cannot be duplicated anywhere else in Canada. When I spoke I was thinking of the opening up of the wilder parts of the country.

Mr. Chairman, in introducing the estimates of the national film board for the current year, it might be helpful to hon. members if I made a brief statement; having in mind particularly the reorganization of the board which took place last year, and its results. '
It will be remembered that, on March 29, 1950, I tabled a report on the national film board by Messrs. J. D. Woods and Gordon Limited, a firm of business consultants. The recommendations made in this report fell into two main categories; (a) those which could be implemented without legislative authority, and (b) those requiring legislative authority before they could be implemented.
In presenting the estimates for the board last year, I informed hon. members of progress with respect to the recommendations in the first category. These have been largely implemented. In particular, I would like to draw attention of hon. members to the consolidation of production services which had been effected.
Following a detailed study by the board of all the activities in which it was engaged, three of these activities were transferred to other departments or agencies where the functions will have more logical application. The displays division has now been taken over by the exhibitions branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce, while the posters and design section and the microfilming section have been absorbed by the king's printer. As a result, the board's activities are now concentrated on the production of films, filmstrips, and still pictures. Furthermore, all three types of production have been placed under one director of production. This
Supply-Resources and Development has resulted in a closer integration of the three services and a reduction in administrative overhead.
In regard to recommendations requiring legislative authority, hon. members will recall that a new National Film Act was enacted by parliament in June of last year. This act:
(a)	Clearly defined the functions of the board.
(b)	Clearly established the board's responsibility to parliament through a designated minister of the crown,
(c)	and reconstituted the board on a basis making it possible to carry out its functions efficiently.
The new National Film Act was proclaimed on October 14 of last year at Which date the new board members took office. We were extremely fortunate in securing the services of the following members, all of whom have great ability as well as wide and varied experience: Mr. Charles S. Band, Toronto, Ont.; Mrs. A. L. Caldwell, Saskatoon, Sask.; Mr. Gratien Gelinas, Montreal, Que.; Mr. A. D. P. Heeney, under secretary of state for external affairs, Ottawa; Mr. Stuart Keate, Victoria, B.C.; Dr. Arthur MacNamara, deputy minister of labour, Ottawa; Mr. Charles Stein, under secretary of state, Ottawa; Dr. Albert W. Trueman, Fredericton, N.B.
I wish to take this opportunity of thanking them for the constructive, energetic and enthusiastic manner in which they have applied themselves to the board's affairs.
As a result of the changes which have taken place, the board's operating efficiency has improved and production has increased while staff has decreased.
Hon. members will be interested in the following comparisons between the operations of last year and those of the preceding year:
As of March 31, 1950, the board's actual working force stood at 577. On March 31, 1951, this force stood at 533, a reduction of approximately 8 per cent.
During the fiscal year recently concluded the board completed 187 film projects of which 130 were full length films of one reel or more. The previous year's figures were 177 and 125 respectively. Production of filmstrips increased from 33 to 48.
The total footage processed by the motion picture laboratory increased 5-4 per cent with a reduction in staff of 7 per cent. The total laboratory output of 11,278,000 feet was the highest for any year since the board was established in 1939.
There were substantial increases in all phases of the distribution field. For example, television bookings increased by 260 per cent.

Members may be interested to learn that, as of May this year, the board had in distribution 62,264 prints, of which 34,017 were in Canada and 28,247 abroad.
There has been a healthy growth in the number of film councils which co-operate with the board in distributing films non-theatrically throughout the dominion. There are now 338 film councils in which 6,670 organizations hold membership. These are serviced by 310 film libraries and the board's non-theatrical films are regularly shown at some 3,300 points across Canada.
The board won nineteen film awards during the year. Six of these were won at the Canadian film awards while the other thirteen were won in countries outside Canada such as the United States, the United Kingdom, and Italy. Members will have seen some of these films during the screenings which are held weekly in one of the committee rooms of the parliament buildings in both English and French.
In presenting the estimates of the board for 1951-52, it will be noted that this year the total figure submitted is $2,602,066, an increase over the preceding year of $307,525. Hon. members will find on page 278 of the estimates the details of services under the various headings of administration, production and distribution.
The increase to which I have referred is occasioned by three factors: (a) The general salary revision which, in the case of the film board, required an additional annual expenditure of $145,000. (b) An increase of $30,000 in the cost of supplies largely resulting from price increases, (c) An item of $250,000 for the introduction of a new international information film program known as the "Freedom Speaks Program." It will be noted that these increases total $425,000-a considerably larger amount than the increased vote asked. This means that the proposed new program, in considerable measure, will be financed through cut-backs in the board's operations.
The primary purpose of the "Freedom Speaks Program" is to try to reflect to peoples of other countries something of the values which we, as a free people, believe to be basic in a democratic society. We propose to employ film as a means not only of depicting and publicizing those principles for which we stand, but of helping at the same time to promote the mutual understanding and solidarity of the free nations.
The program's subject matter will be drawn from the everyday pursuits of Canadians In their work and worship, in their homes


and schools, in their social and political relationships. It will present the drama of ordinary people in a democracy and its approach will be realistic and honest.
To make an interpretative statement on film of the Canadian way of life is by no means easy, but I believe that, in the national film board, there is the capacity and vision to meet this test. Another important factor, when contemplating the possible success of such a program, is that the work of the film board is held in high esteem abroad.
In conclusion, I should like to say that the figures which I mentioned earlier relating to the improvement in output and services indicate the increased efficiency which the new legislation and the new administration of the national film board have achieved. I hope hon. members will share my view that this has been a year of progress and improvement for the board.

I wish to thank the minister for his statement, and I agree with him in regard to the improvement in the board during the year. I think there has been improvement, but there is still room for improvement in that board.

I want to say a few words on the general subject of immigration, and I am taking this opportunity of doing so. My remarks result from a visit to several of our immigration missions abroad and some firsthand knowledge of the problem of displaced persons in Europe. What I shall say on the subject of immigration is not a criticism of our present basic policy; rather it points out the failure of its operation and effectiveness, which is certainly not in any way a reflection on the work being done by members of immigration missions abroad. My statement is based, however, on personal observations of our immigration missions in Germany, Austria and the United Kingdom, as well as visits to several displaced persons camps in various parts of Europe. What I propose to say is, I hope, constructive criticism directed toward the important objective of getting an adequate number of suitable immigrants into Canada with the greatest possible speed in which they can be assimilated.
The subject falls into three main classifications. First, there is the question of the displaced persons and the IRO. Second, there is the problem of population of Germans expelled from other parts of Europe, who are now living on the German and Austrian economies. This is by far the more serious problem at the moment. And third, there is the question of the operation of our immigration policy as carried out at the present time by the department.
Dealing with the displaced persons as distinguished from nationals is at present of minor importance. Nearly all the displaced persons who can be moved have already been dealt with and we are, to use the well-known phrase, now scraping the bottom of the barrel with regard to these camps. As a matter of fact, it can be considered that this problem has been solved as far as it is in our power to do so. The residue now in the camps is almost entirely unacceptable immigrants to Canada. They are unacceptable for several basic reasons. The first of these of course is health.

The residue now in these camps is almost entirely unacceptable as immigrants to Canada. They are unacceptable for several basic reasons. The first of these of course is health. Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
The second bar to these displaced persons is what might be called mental instability. This may follow all the way from reckless irresponsibility, right down to outright insanity. Naturally we should not accept any persons in this category.
The third category contains people Who have had criminal records, who are morally unstable or who are politically dangerous. Here again I would not recommend any loosening of the present regulations.
It has been said that there exist today about 200,000 to 300,000 persons who form the hard core of displaced persons. The solution of this problem is an international one, and we in Canada, who have done proportionately as much as any other nation in the world to assist these unfortunate people, can now help only if we get genuine international action and full co-operation, particularly from the United Nations and the United States, whose record up to now has not been as co-operative as could be desired. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, the new United States regulations have made it much more helpful recently.
Stay with your notes and you will be more accurate.

A suggestion in regard to this problem has been given to me on several occasions, and I give it to the committee as the considered opinion of several officials, both Canadian and European. It is that, first, the hard core does represent an international obligation of the free peoples of the world; second, no country should be asked to accept people who are immediately going to become a charge on that country. Therefore the suggestion made is that an international financial agreement should be made for the care of these people within the countries now sheltering them, who should not become a burden on these countries in which the camps are now situated. This international agreement should, by the provision of funds, jointly bear the cost of providing for the people. When the IRO comes to an end this fall, the remaining displaced persons will become a burden on the economy of the countries in which they are living at the present time and their presence will naturally be resented by these countries.
Coming now to the more serious question of expelled persons of German and Austrian nationality, the situation is far more dangerous. As I have already said in this house at the present session, the impact of this surplus population in Germany, and the damaging effect it has on German economy, is a direct and major cause of the rebirth of nationalism, now called neo-nazism in 80709-308
Germany. Unless this pressure and the unemployment caused by the surplus population are relieved the future of democratic government in Germany is in jeopardy. The German people will no longer believe the pious platitudes about the benefits of democracy if at the same time the democratic world will not help them with this problem which threatens their very ability to survive. This is caused, of course, because western Germany today has been separated from the food-producing areas of the east, which she used to depend on for feeding her population.
What are the figures of this surplus population? The statistics made available by the German government on January 1 show that the number of expelled Germans, including those in the Soviet zone and in Berlin, was 11,396,000 persons. This of course exceeds by nearly 3 million the total number of immigrants absorbed by the whole North American continent during the past 40 years. It is almost equal to the total population of Canada. Of this group, 8,964,000 are directly registered and under the care of the west German government. They are distributed as follows: British zone, 4,811,000; United States zone, 3,839,000; French zone, 314,000. These expellees consist of Germans who in and subsequent to 1945 had to leave areas ceded to the U.S.S.R. and Poland in accordance with the Yalta and Potsdam agreements. They also include the nationals of the Volksdeutsch who were expelled in the same period from Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Rouma-nia and other Soviet satellite countries.
To show how serious this condition is I will give one or two examples.

As I have pointed out, our missions in Germany are inundated with applications and in my opinion the department has not provided those missions with sufficient facilities to handle the tremendous rush. There was a piece in the press the other day that over a thousand Germans a week were coming to Canada and if it is true it would show that the conditions to which I have referred have been remedied. I am speaking on this subject tonight because I feel there is a tremendous job to be done in Europe by our immigration missions.

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
When I was there they certainly were not being provided with the facilities to enable them to do the required job. For instance, there were no X-ray machines in any of our missions on the continent. As has been pointed out, the admission of one immigrant with active tuberculosis lesions may cost this country as much as the cost of operating one of our missions for a whole year. X-ray pictures can be procured in several places in Europe for comparatively small sums and it is extremely difficult for our doctors to spot that the X-ray picture being shown is not in fact the X-ray of the applicant. Our doctors are good at it, but there is no question that some do slip through.
I should like to see our missions equipped with X-ray machines so that our medical staff on the continent may be in complete control of the people to be admitted to Canada. That is extremely important. There were no X-ray machines when I visited our mission in London, tout I understood that some were coming over. It is most important that active cases of tuberculosis be prevented from entering Canada. I certainly would not advocate any relaxation of the regulations and the standards with regard to health.
A word with regard to specialized persons coming to Canada. As I have said, the day of the displaced person is practically over. The best immigrants are the West Germans and there are literally hundreds of thousands who are still anxious to come to Canada. These people are some of the best in Europe today. My criticism is not of the work being done by the mission but rather of the lack of facilities provided to process these immigrants. In the past some of the finest immigrants we had in Canada were of German descent. As a matter of fact if you were looking for a typically Canadian town I doubt very much if you could improve upon the twin cities of Kitchener and Waterloo. A number of those who have contributed greatly to the debates in this house and to the whole Canadian scene politically have been of German dlescent. My former seatmate, the late Karl Homuth, was an example of the second generation Germans who have added so much to the stature and economy of Canada. These people want to come here in their thousands, and I do not believe we have adequately provided1 for their admittance to Canada.
I believe an effort should be made in co-operation with Canadian industry to greatly increase the number of proper types of immigrants from Germany. While I know many representatives of industry have visited our missions, particularly in search of such


people as miners and lumbermen, nevertheless I believe such bodies as the Canadian chamber of commerce and the federations of agriculture, working together with the Department of Labour, could bring about a great speed-up in immigration. I would ask that industry and agriculture co-operate, even to the extent of sending representatives to work with our immigration missions in Europe.
The second point is that in the past we have received a large number of displaced persons, I think over 100,000, who have come to Canada to enter agriculture or domestic service. Many of those people were totally unsuited to work in agriculture, domestic service or the other jobs in which they had agreed to remain. Almost immediately on coming to Canada they became dissatisfied and left their jobs. As a matter of fact many of them remained in their original jobs for only a few weeks, and then left. I believe it was unwise to bring technical and professional people to this country and expect them to make suitable workers in industry, domestic service or other employment. I believe more screening should be done so that this mistake will not be carried on. Personally I have been well satisfied with the displaced persons who have worked for me, but they have told me that out of an entire shipload they were the only people who remained with the same employer until their contract was up. I believe that must be unsatisfactory not only for the displaced person coming to Canada but for the employer as well.
I believe something else should be done when we bring immigrants to this country. When the Ontario scheme was working at Rainbow Corner the prospective immigrant was interviewed and typed, and his ability to do a job was well known before he left England. His papers came ahead of him, and immediately on landing in Canada he had a job and a place to spend the first few days in his new country, so he felt he was being looked after. I realize that the federal authorities carry on that sort of supervision of displaced persons, who upon landing are looked after at places like Ajax before they proceed to the labour offices and are given employment. I believe an immigrant should be made to feel that he is wanted, that his abilities should be known, that a job should be arranged and that for the first few days in this country he should be looked after. I realize that this would mean a considerable expansion in the department, but there is no more important job to be done in connection with our new citizens than to make them feel they are welcome in their new home. I feel

that what the Ontario government did at Rainbow Corner could be copied with profit by the federal government. I know a great many immigrants are looked after by relatives or friends, or by industry; but I have heard of many others who on coming to Canada have landed cold at some station not knowing where to go, and have had to be looked after by one society or another. I believe that is a mistake, and that looking after the immigrants and providing for their immediate employment is of enormous importance.
I have just one other suggestion to make to the minister. There is still in Germany if not a feeling of hostility at least a refusal to accept responsibility for the last war. I should like to see all the immigrants who come from Bavaria and the district around Munich forced to go through the concentration camp at Dachau to see the evidence of the crimes committed at that concentration camp by the nazis. I know it is impossible, but I think it would be a salutary thing for those immigrants.
I want to say again, Mr. Chairman, that this problem is of enormous importance. First of all, the problem of the displaced person, and secondly the expelled surplus population of Germany, are going to upset the economy of Germany and prevent European recovery unless something is done. Then, you have the problem of obtaining the right type of immigrant in sufficient numbers, bringing them rapidly to Canada and putting them into suitable employment. There never were such hardworking people as the minister's staff in Berlin. They were working eleven, twelve and sometimes sixteen hours a day. The various teams visited the camps and travelled many thousands of miles a week. I feel that steps should be taken, if they have not been taken already, to assist those people who are working so hard and doing a good job for Canada. These doctors, the security people and others, should be able to work the normal hours of other professions.

I should like to put a question to the hon. gentleman. Can he tell us whether these Germans whom he wishes to import into Canada are people who were reared in the democratic way of life known to us in Canada, or were they brought up with the totalitarian philosophy of life?

No one in Europe is brought up with what we know as the democratic philosophy of life. Here I want to say that the Germans today are as democratic as any people in Europe. The fact that they had national socialism is, I believe, a salutary

There are

To deal with
the numbers first, the officers in Canada total 314. When the immigrants come forward they are in roughly three categories: Those who have been sponsored in the first place and have a direct destination to which to go to enter into employment at once, and there are the dependents of that group. Then, there is another group who have come forward because they are entitled to come by our laws and seek employment when they arrive here. The latter group constitutes much the smallest group of all, and they usually have facilities of their own. Nevertheless, we have settlement offices and settlement officers in practically all parts of Canada to which immigrants go, who make it their business to receive those people, to see that they have facilities to use pending their getting employment and generally assisting them in getting that employment.

But the figures for this year show that there has been a decided increase in immigration to Canada over the comparable period in 1950. For example, beginning in November of last year the figures show that from that time until the end of May, 74,247 immigrants came to Canada as compared with 41,863 in the same period of the preceding year. The total numbers for the first five months of this year were 60,356. This represents an increase of 99 per cent over the corresponding months of 1950.
99 per cent?

Yes, 99 per cent. The February, March and April totals were the highest for these months during the post-war period; and the May total of 20,254 was the highest for any month since the
(Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood).]
end of the war, 4,931 above the previous record month of June, 1948, when 15,323 immigrants entered Canada. The total of 60,356 for the five months ended May 31, 1951, exceeded by 18,404 the total of 41,952 during the comparable period of 1948, during which year 125,414 immigrants entered this country. In point of fact, arrivals during June will result in a figure for the six' months ending June 30 which will exceed the total of 73,912 who came here during the entire year of 1950.
I think perhaps those are the figures my hon. friend wanted.
From the time of confederation-and I do not mean with respect to Newfoundland but rather general confederation-is there much difference between the figure for immigration and that for emigration?

It is quite true that in the period of the 1880's and the early 1890's there was an excess of emigration over immigration; and it is quite true that the same condition obtained after the first world war for a short time. I am informed that until perhaps the first world war there was not a great difference in the figures spread over the period from confederation. But dealing with the present, since the end of the second world war, the numbers who have come here have greatly exceeded the numbers who have left this country.

May I ask the minister this
question: In his opinion, from his knowledge of the department, how much more of population can Canada absorb?

I am sure that
the committee would be interested to know what opinion the hon. member for St. John's East holds on that point. There are distinguished members of the House of Commons who have expressed opinions, including the leader of the party to which he belongs. My recollection is that the leader of his party has said that this country can maintain between 50 million and 100 million people.
What does the minister say?

The minister
says that, for the moment, he is considering the year 1951-52 or the year 1951, during the course of which we are contemplating a figure of somewhere between 100,000 and 150,000 people coming into this country. We feel that they can be absorbed into the economy this year.

interesting statement which the minister has

made. Can he give us a break-down of the immigrants by countries of origin? That would be best. Inasmuch as so many of them have come from displaced persons camps, it would be better if you have the break-down of them by countries from which they originally came.

I should like to ask the minister if he has given any further consideration to the problem of allowing children over 21 years of age of Canadian Chinese to come 
into Canada? I realize that this has been an extremely difficult problem. It has taken quite a long time to look over the cases of all these Chinese children.

Will the hon. member
speak a little bit louder?

I am speaking of the problem of Chinese immigration. As the minister will realize, it has been quite difficult to look over all the cases. In some cases the children who were then eligible to come to Canada have now become 21 and it is not possible for them to come in under the present regulations. I was wondering if the minister had anything new to give to the House of Commons in regard to that matter.

As the committee knows, P.C. 2115 governs the admission to Canada of immigrants who are children of Canadian citizens of Chinese origin. That order in council permits the entry of unmarried children to the age of 21 years. We have found that, in some -cases, there have been evidences of real hardship and perhaps suffering if that rule were to be applied rigidly. It has been applied rigidly, Mr. Chairman, and I do not know of any exceptions which have -been made to it up to -the present time. Nevertheless, there have been cases -presented to me by hon. members, including the hon. member for Comox-Al-berni-
And the hon. member for Kamloops.

-the hon. member for Kamloops and many others. Having in mind the present situation in China and the known desire of parents to have their children with them, we have come to the conclusion that we will give consideration to those cases of unmarried children over 21 up to the age of 25, to see if the circumstances warrant their admission on the grounds I have stated.

If one of His
Majesty's ministers will accept a suggestion from a humble member of the opposition, whil-e I admire the neatness of the answer he gave to the hon. member for St. John's East a moment ago, in confining himself entirely to this year, I suggest that the minister in charge of immigration will have to have a view a little beyond that, because those who are thinking of coming to this country will want to know something of his views not perhaps in tens of millions -but at any rate some indication of what he thinks on this subject. B-ut that is merely i-n passing.
The question I want to ask the minister is this. He has told us he has 314 establishments in his own department, I understand. Will he say something about co-operation? Let us take the province of Ontario, for example, and the provincial authorities. Do they have any organization of their own?
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Do they collaborate in any way? If so, what is their organization? There is a second branch of this matter that I wish to inquire into, but I will ask those questions first.

All provincial governments have a department in which there is some officer responsible for immigration, although all provincial governments do not, in fact, engage directly in it. To take the question with respect to the province of Ontario, there is a department there which has been actively interested in immigration.
I think I can say that between that depart- [DOT] ment, this department and the Department of Labour of this government there is the closest co-operation to see that the needs of any particular industry that specifically wants help will get it; or alternatively, to see that there is a general flow of acceptable and desirable immigrants to that province. I can only add that all the steps that have -been taken by this department have been discussed with -the representatives of the province of Ontario, and with other provinces from time to time, as the circumstances may require. And we are sometimes rivals perhaps in the field under certain circumstances, but only rivals in order to have the most advantageous kind of immigrants.
Is there any relaxation of the rules concerning the adopted children of Chinese coming into Canada?
Adopted children of anyone.

We have not been able to make any relaxation in that rule yet, and might I explain why. Immigration to Canada from China has been on the increase since the beginning of the year. The numbers that are coming forward are quite substantial. The figure for last year was I think about 1,741. That will be exceeded substantially this year, so that our facilities at Hong Kong are limited, and we have felt that as long as there are unmarried children who come within the regulations, and as long as there is this other group I have just mentioned, we could not go outside of that, until at least the future should make it desirable to make the exception my hon. friend has suggested.
Will the minister tell us what inspection facilities there are at Hong Kong and what medical facilities for the purpose of examining those children who are brought forward?

Early this year it was evident that the number of approved applications from Canada were not being dealt with so that the backlog would be brought down in Hong Kong, and we sent

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration additional inspectors and stenographic help to that office. The office consists of inspectors and clerical staff. The medical staff is a local medical staff from whom we get our reports. We are processing now somewhere between 200 and 250 applications a month in Hong Kong and feel that that is adequate at the moment, because in fact the numbers did drop in May just a few. We think that perhaps we have reached the peak of the present group of applications, and we can handle them satisfactorily in the future.

I want to come back to the question I was asking the minister. He half anticipated the further question I was going to ask by mentioning himself the fact that the labour department also has certain staff which deals with this same problem. Perhaps the minister can tell me how many of these officers are in Ontario; that is, of the department of immigration, how many of the 314 officers are in Ontario, how many of them were there last year? How many officers has the labour department? How many officers would the department of Ontario have? The minister very frankly used the word "rivalry" which of course was in my mind. I would be very glad if he would give us these figures. Then there is one other thing. What is the size of his staff, not merely the number of officers, but the size of the staff? For purposes of simplification, let us take Ontario.
There are 64 offices in Ontario, and 469 on the staff in Ontario.

I should like to suggest to the minister that in the interests of immigration he go into a huddle with the Minister of Resources and Development and with the Minister of Defence Production. Unquestionably we need in Canada today a great many skilled workers, particularly from the British isles. I understand that they are being brought into this country in considerable numbers. At the A. V. Roe plant near Toronto there are several hundred of these skilled workers from the British isles. They tell me that the housing situation in the Toronto district was very much misrepresented to them before they came. These men now have to live at considerable distances from the plant. As a matter of fact, they live all over the city. They pay as much as $120 a month for accommodation, and are very discontented over having to live under these conditions. These are skilled mechanics. They tell me that they are quite willing to build their own houses and to assume the financial responsibility for the building of them if the government will give them some fMr. Harris (Grey-Bruce).]
help, in securing either the land or the materials. Even under the new regulations, they are somewhat limited as to the amount of money they can bring into the country, but they have all the skills necessary. They are quite prepared to build their own houses in their off hours, and they are anxious that the government shall give them some co-operation by way of making land available for which they can pay over a period of time. Has the minister given any thought to that? I am sure that something of that kind would encourage these people, who are very desirable immigrants and are very essential.
Before we get away from the Chinese question may I ask the minister what are the qualifications of Chinese immigrants between the ages of 17 and 25?

Between the ages of 17 and 21, they are admissible upon proof that they are in fact children of the applicant here. I have just explained the policy we are to follow in the future with respect to those over 21. I hope my hon. friend heard me. If he did not, I can explain to him later.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Perhaps the minister would take a moment longer to comment on the other points that were brought to his attention in the memorandum recently presented to him by the group representing the Chinese. I hold in my hand a copy of the memorandum, but I will not take the time to read it. If he does not have his copy with him I can send him mine. I can say to the minister that there are about five headings. He can get the gist of each point by looking at the headings, and I would appreciate his comment on the five points dealt with in the memorandum.

I want to remind the minister that I asked him a triplebarrelled question, and he answered only one-third of it. I asked how many officers of the department of immigration there were in Ontario, how many in the Department of Labour, and how many in the department of immigration of Ontario, and he answered only the part about his own department.

I would not want to misinform the committee on anything in the Department of Labour. I am sure the minister can inform the committee correctly on that. With respect to the officers of the provincial government, I do not know of any except those in the city of Toronto in connection with the provincial capital. We deal with the office at that place; and that, so far as I know, is the only office they have.
Will the minister explain how the rivalry works?

I think I made it clear that I said it was a friendly rivalry for the best type of immigrant. The Ontario government has been seeking to obtain immigrants by selection abroad-and in London, particularly-for persons who require their services here. There is no rivalry, in the sense that we are not hunting the same person; but there is a demand at Ontario House in London for immigrants for Ontario, as there is a demand at our headquarters in London for immigrants for the whole of Canada. To that extent there may be some rivalry in seeking persons for this country. But we do not seek a person for the same applicant.
We hope.

I should like to ask two or three questions, the first of which has to do with the inspectional facilities at Hong Kong. Has the minister anything to say as to the efficacy of X-ray methods to determine the age of children? I know of certain cases where children have been applied for by bona fide Chinese residents in Canada, and they have been refused admission on the ground that the X-rays determined that the ages were not those specified in the applications. What medical facilities are available at Hong Kong in connection with inspections of that kind? The minister did not refer to the question of X-rays. Is he prepared to say that the X-ray method is sufficient to establish the age of a child?
I am not sure whether the hon. member for Kamloops fully understands the procedure at the Hong Kong office.

You will have to fully
explain it.

What happens is this. We approve of an application in Canada by a Chinese resident here for a child. That application is forwarded to the Hong Kong office. The parent here is notified that it has been approved; and both the Hong Kong office and no doubt the parent notify the child to appear in the Hong Kong office for examination.
As the hon. member knows, there are no birth records in China. When our inspector interviews a young man who says that he is the son referred to in the application, he is obliged by our regulations to determine whether in fact that is the son of the person in this country. He can do that only by his estimation of the age, to see if it corresponds with the age stipulated in the application, and by asking questions as to the family connections, and by any other 80709-309J
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration form of examination which would elicit facts to correspond with the application.
It happens that in some cases our inspector comes to the conclusion that the boy who presents himself is of a quite different age from that of the son in question. The boy is informed to that effect by our inspector. If he disputes the decision of the inspector he is told that if he would like to go to his own medical practitioner in Hong Kong and have an X-ray taken it might indicate that our inspector was wrong, and that the age was as stated in the application. When he does that those X-rays are read by the local practitioner who takes them, by our inspector and, ultimately, by our officials here in the Department of National Health and Welfare.
As to the efficacy of X-ray examination, speaking generally it would appear that they are reasonably accurate for our purposes. We are dealing with a group of people who, at least up to the present time, are under twenty-one. And while, as I am sure the hon. member for Lanark would agree, there can be a difference of opinion about almost anything in the medical world, there is nevertheless a reasonable certainty that these X-rays can give a clear indication, within certain limits, of the age of any person in that age group.

Let us suppose that a prospective immigrant boy is able to answer the questions regarding his family connections. In those circumstances are the X-rays relied upon exclusively? In other words, if in the opinion of the medical officer the X-rays disclose a difference in age, would they be relied upon exclusively, in spite of the fact that the boy was able to answer the other questions satisfactorily?

We begin with the fact that, even if the examination has been satisfactory so far as the information is concerned, and if after that our inspector concludes that the age of the boy is not that of the supposed son, it is at that point that he is given the option of having X-rays taken to see if they will convince the inspector that he has estimated the age incorrectly. We have had cases where applicants have answered examinations with reasonable satisfaction, but the X-rays have shown them to be four or five years beyond the ages stipulated in the applications.

Mr. Chairman, I have received several complaints from farmers in western Canada regarding immigrants who, apparently, had come out under contract to work for so many months, so as to repay the money advanced for their fares. The complaints

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration were that many of them did not stay the specified time, so that the farmers were out the amount of money advanced.
Has this experience been general? In cases where it has happened, has it always been the immigrant who was to blame or, on the other hand, have some of those immigrants been asked to live under conditions under which they should not have been expected to live. Could the minister say whether that policy is being followed today?

Mr. Chairman, so far as the government's assisted passage scheme is concerned, I doubt if the persons my hon. friend mentioned would have been under that scheme. The plan went into effect only on February 1, and I suppose the persons about whom he has spoken came forward to farmers who prepaid their passages so as to get them out here.

Apparently the inspector went out to inspect the accommodation before the immigrants came; so it must have been under a government plan of some kind. The farms were inspected before the farmers were allowed to have the immigrants.

If a farmer has applied for a farm worker, we inspect the premises to see if (a) he needs the worker and (b) he has reasonably good facilities for accommodation. That is part of the preliminary inquiry as to whether the application will be approved or not.
Having done that, the information with respect to conditions is given to the immigrant abroad. We may not go into great detail, but I want to assure the committee that we do not paint a rosy picture if there is not one there. If at that time the local employer, in order to expedite the coming of the immigrant, chooses to advance money, that is his own responsibility. We do not ask him to do it-although we are often asked if they should.
At the present time I understand the government puts up the money. The farmer is not asked to put up the money at all.
Since February 1, the plan has been in operation, and is just beginning to function.

Referring back to the discussion of the X-ray method, may I ask the minister if it is not a fact that the American immigration authorities have discarded the X-ray method of checking with respect to Oriental immigrants?

I am not aware of that although it has been stated during debates in this house. We have found X-ray

examination to be reasonably accurate for our purposes and I think it will be continued.

Could a greater
number of immigrants be sent to British Columbia and north of Edmonton? I looked over the records some time ago and found that some 3,000 had come to Ontario, a similar number to Quebec, but only a few hundred to British Columbia. It is most important that white population be placed in the valleys that face the Pacific coast. Is the department getting any co-operation from the government of British Columbia in respect to settlement, from the transcontinental railroad who paid great attention to settlement in former years and from the Northern Alberta Railway which is supposed to be a colonization road running from Edmonton into the Peace river country and to the north.

At the moment the great emphasis on immigration is for workers rather than for land settlers. Nevertheless we recognize that British Columbia and the Peace river area offer a good field for settlement. We have taken steps to see if we can get people to go there as part of our settlement scheme. To that end we have continued the pre-war close arrangement with the railroads to bring forward settlers on terms which perhaps are rather detailed. We do encourage the railroads to continue the colonization schemes they had prior to the war.
With respect to the immediate future we have made a decision which I think will aid my hon. friend in the plans he has in mind. We have provided that the Canadian government will absorb the differential in the cost of inland rail transportation between points west of Winnipeg for immigrants who come to Canada under the assisted passage loan scheme, provided they stay in the class of employment for which they are selected for a period of one year. Our reason for doing that is the reason my hon. friend has given, because a large percentage of the immigrants have been coming to Quebec and Ontario.

I wonder if I might refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Battle River who asked some questions with regard to the entry of adopted children of Chinese. I know that this concerns only a small number of Chinese children but I am sure the minister has had brought to his attention these unfortunate cases of children who have been adopted by Chinese in Canada. I wonder if he would put this matter up to his cabinet colleagues and ask them to pass an order in council granting permission to these adopted children to enter Canada, provided the minister is satisfied that they are really the adopted

children of Chinese citizens of Canada. I doubt if there would be more than fifty or one hundred children involved. As I have made clear in the past, I am opposed to unlimited Chinese immigration, but I think there are strong compassionate grounds for permitting such children to enter.
Are Chinese now living here exempt from military service? Are Chinese who are coming in under this new policy exempt from military service?

I am not aware of any exemption from military service except of those groups which were admitted by order in council under a special arrangement in 1898. There may be certain Men-nonites and what are commonly known as Doukhobors in this class.

I hope the minister will consider the representations with regard to the adopted children of Chinese, but that is not what I really rose to ask. We have had some interesting figures regarding immigration and I should like to know if there have been any deportations in the last year and, if so, for what causes. I ask this because of the letter I received some months ago complaining that some of the immigrants were afraid they might be deported if they applied for public assistance.

That information appears in the annual report for the year ended March 31, 1950. The total number deported was 422, for the following reasons:
Medical cases	 50
Public charges	 33
Criminality	 103
Other civil cases	 230
Dependents accompanying those deported.. 6

There is a medical examination in the country of origin and it seems to me that if we examine these people medically and accept them we are under obligation to permit them to remain. It seems to me that to deport these people is creating a great hardship after they have been allowed to come to the country.
Could the minister give the details of the other civil cases?
Most of those wouldi he deserters from ships who have been picked up and ordered deported.

This question was raised the other day by the hon. member for Kootenay West, and I was quite surprised when it was addressed to me, since in the past questions having to do with the Doukhobors have been addressed to the Minister of Justice. I cannot possibly let these remarks go without saying a word. I have a number of Doukhobors in my constituency, and I want to say they are some of the finest people who ever came to Canada. They are good, industrious, clean and fine farmers; and just because the Sons of Freedom have gone bad, as you might say, is no reason why anyone should get up in this house and say things about the Doukhobors who came to this country to make homes for themselves. I want to make it quite clear that I agree with the hon. member who has just spoken that the Doukhobors are good farmers indeed. Unfortunately the group to which I referred have become the subject of some controversy in my province. All I am asking is whether the federal government has any responsibility in the matter of their movement or resettlement, and I understand the minister to say the federal government has no responsibility in that connection.
My answer was that this branch of the government has no concern with that matter.
The minister did not answer my suggestion that he discuss with the government the matter of the admissibility of adopted minor children of Canadians of Chinese ancestry.

Cases have been brought to my attention in which it would appear that Chinese parents in this country are applying for the admission of children who have been adopted while one parent or the other was in China. It is difficult to determine just how far these adoptions have taken the form of what we would consider western adoptions rather than those which are common in the east; nevertheless the government is at all times ready to give consideration to any matter raised by an hon. member, and I promise to give consideration to what has been said by the hon. gentleman.

In saying what I did about German immigration I would not want it to be taken from my remarks that I would not welcome the greatest possible percentage of British immigrants. When I was in London there was a backlog of some 50,000 names in the Ontario office of people who had indicated that they wanted to come to Canada, but were waiting because of financial or other reasons. A tremendous number of British people want to come to Canada, and I hope they will come.


Then I have one more suggestion to offer the minister. I suggest that he send to his missions pictures of the king and queen, of these parliament buildings and possibly of this chamber.
How about George Drew?

That is a bright one. I make that suggestion because of an incident that occurred while I was in Salzburg, where the picture of the Prime Minister was on the wall. One of the Czech immigrants, not knowing who it was, asked another, and the reply was, "That is Juan Peron." The first one replied, "Well, where is Evita?" It is not quite dignified for the Prime Minister to be mistaken for Peron. I suggest there is nothing the European so admires about Canada, apart from its physical attributes, as our form of government and our monarch. So I think the minister would be well advised if he had pictures such as I mentioned displayed at the missions, setting out very clearly the type of government we have here. Several prospective immigrants suggested to me they had no idea what form of government we had in Canada.
How many of those have come through the assisted passage? I think the assisted passage scheme, so far as I can understand it, is a good one.
It is not possible to say yet. The number of warrants which have come forward total only 1,840 because of the time lag, and a large percentage of those are from the United Kingdom.

I asked the question because I was under the impression that the minister had stated on earlier occasions that a request had been made that the government of the United Kingdom give consideration to the relaxation of the restriction on funds. Is that not correct?
I said that a year ago. I said that we were going to do so.

The reason I ask that question is that on Thursday, April 26, there appears the following question and answer in the Hansard of the British House of Commons:
No. 54. Mr. Leather: To ask Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, what requests the Canadian government has made to His Majesty's government to increase the present amount of transferable funds for emigrants; when such requests were made; and what action His Majesty's government has taken.

Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, we are not understanding the use of our own words. In the speech I made a year ago I did suggest that our troubles lay partly in the restrictions on currency, and I expressed the hope that those restrictions would be lifted. I do not know whether or not that would be a formal application, but it was a statement of the hopes of this government that the restrictions would be lifted. I have repeated that on many occasions since. I have no reason to doubt that those representations were known, because they were debated in the house at Westminster.

There is a vast difference between a statement being made in this house and representations being made. I simply asked the question in view of this question and answer to which I have referred. Were formal representations made by the Canadian government to the government of the United Kingdom requesting relaxation of their restrictions on the transfer of funds by immigrants coming to Canada?
The answer is no.

Perhaps again we are misunderstanding each other, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member asked me a moment ago if formal representations had been made. I thought he meant at that time, in April, and I answered no. Formal representations have been made since that time, leading I take it to the announcement which was made the other day in the house at Westminster. Should there be any doubt about the situation with respect to immigration from the United Kingdom, I should like to point out that we have at the moment 35,346 British subjects who have had their applications for immigration to this country approved. This has been due in large part, I think, to the increased interest in immigration which became apparent about November, perhaps October of last year. Now, it may very well be that the number greatly increased when we announced the assisted passage scheme in late December. At any rate, all winter our officers have seen a substantial increase in the number that they have handled. We think the announcement made the other day will stimulate the numbers who will apply, although there was no sign of let-up before the announcement was made.
Nevertheless, it would appear that we are in agreement that the currency restrictions did bring about the drop in numbers applying in the late 1948, 1949 and early in 1950, but numbers applied before the present change in restrictions.

How many points are now available to the immigrants on the continent of Europe? At what points may immigrants be examined who wish to leave the continent of Europe? Have some new points of examination been added?

We have officers at Athens, Berne, Brussels, Copenhagen, Hanover, Karlsruhe, Paris, Rome, Salzburg, Stockholm and the Hague.
IMr. Drew.]
In order that we may be quite clear on what has taken place, on what date was the formal representation made to which the minister now refers, and what was the nature of that representation?

Mr. Chairman, I do not think I should disclose the representations which were made, except to say that they were to the effect that we would hope that the British government would ease the restrictions. The formal representations were made since the Secretary of State for External Affairs left a week ago.
So that the first formal representation that has been made by the government under this new department is within the past week?
I beg your pardon, Mr. Chairman; the formal representations were made in May and were followed up by the Secretary of State for External Affairs since.

speechtext: May I ask the minister if there are any currency restrictions in France that would affect French immigrants? And are there any currency restrictions in Belgium and Holland which would affect immigrants to this country?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The minister has said that some representations have been made to the United Kingdom government in the hope of obtaining relaxation of the currency regulations. Have some similar representations been made to the governments of France, Belgium and Holland?
No formal representations have been made; but as I pointed out a while ago, I have repeatedly made statements that we would hope that these currency restrictions would be lifted.
May I ask the minister if he is ready to give an answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Peterborough West with regard to the deportation of Fred Rose?

Fred Rose was convicted and sentenced to prison for an

offence under the Official Secrets Act. At the time that was done the citizenship act was so worded that it did not cover that particular crime as one which could be used to revoke his citizenship. When the citizenship act was introduced into this house in the fall, I take it, of 1946 the provision was made that citizenship might be revoked with respect to a person who has shown himself by act or speech to be disaffected or disloyal to His Majesty. There was a lengthy debate in the house, in which many opposition members contended that that was too broad a definition, with the result that an amendment was presented by one of the opposition members, and the section was amended to read as follows:
A person who has been convicted of treason or sedition by a court of competent jurisdiction.
That was the state of the law at the time of this conviction. The result was that Fred Rose could not have his citizenship revoked under the law as it was at that time. The committee will remember that this year we amended the law to put it substantially in the words in which it had been first introduced into the house. But at that time I pointed out that it was not retroactive and would not affect Fred Rose. The result is that he cannot have his citizenship revoked under the law at the present time. That brings the further result that you cannot deport a person who has Canadian citizenship.

I want to be clear about this school at Moose Factory, because it raises a question which has been referred to by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, namely, the desirability of attaining some uniform standards or some uniform standard right across the country, which is in keeping with the general educational levels.

I should like to make some suggestions to the parliamentary assistant in connection with the administration of this branch. I am not objecting to the amount of the vote, but I think arrangements could be made that would facilitate the movement of cattle from the western provinces to feeder farms in Ontario. A year or two ago arrangements were made whereby an Ontario farmer could purchase a carload or carloads of cattle in the western provinces and have them needled in Winnipeg for t.b. If three days had elapsed before they arrived at his own farm and the results were known the cattle could be retained. If that time had not elapsed, they would be held in the Ontario yards at Toronto. I think that was a very good arrangement. At the present time if an Ontario farmer wishes to purchase a carload of feeder cows, that arrangement does not apply. I think it would be a service to Ontario feeders if the same arrangement applied to feeder cows that applies at present to feeder heifers. At the present time these cows are unloaded at Toronto, needled, and held there for three days. The objection is not so much because of the cost of keeping the cattle there as because they are exposed to disease, particularly what we farmers call shipping fever. This is something that could be remedied very easily, so these cows could go through without being exposed to this disease. When a farmer comes to the yards at Toronto and wants to buy a truckload of cattle, he might take nine or ten feeder steers and perhaps three or four dairy

heifers, as they are termed by the veterinary. The steers can be bought and a clearance obtained to take them out, but they hold the dairy heifers for three days until the tests are completed. Again these cattle are exposed to such diseases as shipping fever with which those yards are reeking, particularly in the fall when they are handling many carloads a day.
I suggest to the department that it is time for a change. Probably this procedure had its place in the past but it has served its purpose now that the whole province is tested, so I do not see why these dairy heifers should be held, particularly at a time when we need more dairy cows. I know from my own experience and the conversations I have had with commission men in the yards at Toronto that many sales are lost of heifers which ordinarily would be taken to the country. I also suggest that the facilities at Ontario yards, which are under the control of federal health of animals branch, should be improved. There are not enough needling pens. In the fall when there is a considerable run of stockers the facilities are quite insufficient, and many people are inconvenienced by not being able to get their stock out the day it is purchased. These are some things I think might very well be taken care of and improved.

notice that taken together the two items in the estimates amount to about $15 million. We are very glad to support this, but I point out that when $65 million was voted to the western farmers a short time ago as compensation, some people misunderstood it. That covered a period of five years, or an average of $13 million a year. This vote is $15 million for one year. We are glad to support it because we think it is in the interests of agriculture generally, but I want to bring that point to the attention of the committee.

This is a matter on which I would like to comment for a considerable time, but will not do so tonight because of the lateness of the session. I quite agree that this is important to agriculture. Without discussing the merits of the $65 million vote I want to state that in my opinion and I think in the opinion of anyone who has any knowledge of eastern agriculture scarcely any expenditure that could be made by the government would result in a greater production. You may spend a few million dollars on this item. I have the figures, and if I were not patient and respectful of this committee I would have them put on the record to show that hundreds of millions of dollars of increased production have resulted from this expenditure.
I have one regretful suggestion with respect to this. Each year we have to wait until the supplementary estimates come down before we know whether these payments are to be continued for another year. This is one of the most important factors contributing to the success of at least the dairy industry and poultry industry-I will not say eastern Canada because I am not competent to say that, but I can say in the maritime provinces. I know that the producers of those two foodstuffs have been anxiously awaiting the supplementary estimates to ascertain whether the payments were included. I would urge upon the parliamentary assistant and the government that this matter should be incorporated as a permanent feature of our agricultural economy. We should not be dependent upon yearly grants, and waiting in doubt and uncertainty. This expires at the end of July, and we are now almost at the end of June. We do not know until these estimates come down whether the matter will be covered. I want to put that on the record.
I also notice that the amount for this year included in the general estimates comes to $15 million, whereas last year I believe it was $18 million or $18-5 million. Can the parliamentary assistant tell us what the reason is for the decrease in the vote?

I should like to point out to the house that owing to the fact no support was given potatoes last fall in the provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, thousands of bushels are now being dumped. At a late date this spring they did give us support through the starch factories, but those factories have not been able to take care of all the potatoes. Good potatoes are now past being ground into starch and they are being dumped daily. That is what is taking place with good foodstuff the price of which is so high in Canada. It is being dumped. I should like to ask the minister why no support was given to the potato crop or with respect to the surplus potatoes this last fall when it was asked for?
