speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Naturally this is a matter of government policy. They committed themselves to the extent of $300,000. That was the extent to which they committed themselves.

Would the parliamentary
assistant say that $300,000 compared with the $65 million given to western Canada? The

Supply-Agriculture
sum of $300,000 is enough for the maritimes, but you do not stop at any $300,000 when it is to go to the west. When potatoes were selling for 20 cents a bushel last fall, I want to know why these growers were not protected in Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Farmers under the Veterans Land Act were forced to sell their potatoes last fall at 20 cents a bushel. Those farmers had no relief whatever. Those who were able to hold their potatoes until spring had some relief as a result of the starch program. But the starch factories in the maritime provinces were not able to grind all those potatoes until they became too bad for starch purposes. Now those potatoes are being dumped. Thousands of bushels of good food are being dumped. This is something which should have been taken care of by the government or by the agricultural prices support board last fall.

I think that question is one that really ought to be answered by the Department of Agriculture. I realize that the parliamentary assistant is at a disadvantage in undertaking to deal with this matter; but it seems to me that sooner or later-and perhaps the sooner the better-we in Canada must decide what agricultural commodities are going to be supported under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, and when they are going to be supported; that is, at what prices it will become necessary to support them.
We must regularize this matter of the support of agricultural products from coast to coast in Canada. Just such a remark as that which the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton has made is thoroughly understandable and thoroughly justifiable as long as we have no regular policy announced and understood throughout the country. If the parliamentary assistant has the information, I wish he would tell us when the dominion government would be prepared to support potatoes. We fully realize that to the maritime provinces this is important. Once more we see some people making light of this matter. I do not know when the time is going to come when the members of the House of Commons are going to realize that the welfare of Ontario and Quebec depends on the welfare of the maritime provinces.
And Alberta too.

That is perfectly right. I thought that hon. members would know the rest of it. I could name the others. That is perfectly true. We should know what we can count on. As I say, I have a great deal of sympathy for the maritime provinces because they are specializing in potatoes for several reasons, one of them, I suppose, being

their climate and the other their soil. We certainly should have some over-all policy under which we shall say to the producers of potatoes in the maritime provinces that when the price of potatoes falls below a certain point we are going to support them with assistance; and it should be fairly well known what that point is, why that point is chosen, how much assistance will be given and why. Has the parliamentary assistant any information that he can give the committee as a basis upon which to work from here on?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I will admit that that is an extremely difficult question to answer. Nevertheless supports are given to assist and to help any industry that is in difficulty. Potatoes are a difficult product to support because they are grown everywhere and anywhere. The United States tried price support for them, and had a formula for the purpose, but they had to stop after spending a few hundreds of millions of dollars. The only formula that we can go by is that we will endeavour to support any product under a marketing board or assist a marketing board of a province so as to help the board set up by each province in Canada. 1 know about the one in respect to our own province of Ontario. It is only assistance, to assist them in order that they might in their wisdom, through these boards, be able to try to meet their own difficulty if that is at all possible. But we should try to help and to assist them if it is possible to do so.
When the Minister of Agriculture put this act through the house in 1944 he made the statement that no agricultural product would be dumped during the time that he was Minister of Agriculture.
But that was before an election.

Yes. It was before the election in 1945. The department of agriculture of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island met a delegation from this department; and a delegation from the marketing board and the board counsel of those two provinces made a great many trips up here last fall when potatoes were selling for 20 cents a bushel. That was the time to remove the surplus from the market. If something had been done at that time with regard to the starch program, we would not have to dump potatoes today. Last fall was the time to do something.

As I understood the parliamentary assistant, he stated that support might be given or could be given when the product had been marketed under the provisions of a marketing act. We have that situation in Nova Scotia, with the marketing of

apples under the Nova Scotia marketing board and the marketing act. I would ask the parliamentary assistant if he is prepared to state what assistance the government or his department is prepared to give the Nova Scotia apple growers for the losses sustained during the preceding season.
